sk: उशन् ह वै वाजश्रवसः सर्ववेदसं ददौ | तस्य ह नचिकेता नाम पुत्र आस ||
ro: uśan · ha · vai · vājaśravasaḥ · sarvavedasaṁ · dadau | tasya · ha · naciketā · nāma · putra · āsa ||
hi: वाजश्रवस् ने (यश की कामना से) विश्वजित् यज्ञ में अपना सम्पूर्ण धन दान कर दिया। उसका नचिकेता नाम का एक पुत्र था।
en: Vajashravasa, desirous of reward, gave away all his possessions (in the Vishvajit sacrifice). He had a son named Nachiketa.

ws.e: desiring — present participle of √vaś ('to wish, desire'); wanting heavenly reward
Vajashravasa — patronymic: 'descendant of Vajashravas'; also called Gautama/Aruni in some recensions
all possessions — sarva (all) + vedas (wealth, property); everything he owned
gave away — perfect of √dā ('to give'); a completed, irreversible act
Nachiketa — the boy's name; possibly from na+ciketa ('not yet known/conscious') or naci+ketas ('fire of consciousness')

gr: uśan — present participle of √vaś: 'desiring,' 'wishing for.' This immediately sets the moral context: Vajashravasa's sacrifice is motivated by desire for reward, not by pure devotion. sarvavedasam dadau — 'gave away all possessions': the Vishvajit sacrifice requires giving away everything. But the next verse will reveal the gift was hollow. naciketā nāma putra āsa — 'he had a son named Nachiketa': the simple naming introduces the true hero.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.1.1 — The opening verse establishes the moral tension: a sacrifice performed for selfish desire (uśan) using worthless gifts. Nachiketa's name itself may encode the theme — 'the fire of inquiry' or 'that which is not yet known.'

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि 'उशन्' (कामना करते हुए) शब्द ही इस यज्ञ की सीमा बता देता है — सकाम कर्म स्वर्ग तो दे सकता है पर मोक्ष नहीं। नचिकेता की कथा निष्काम ज्ञान की यात्रा है जो सकाम कर्म के भीतर से उत्पन्न होती है।
advaita.en: Shankara notes that 'uśan' (desiring) immediately limits the sacrifice — desire-motivated action can yield heaven but not liberation. Nachiketa's story is the journey of desireless knowledge arising from within desire-motivated ritual.
advaita.ins: Even flawed spiritual practice can produce genuine seekers — Nachiketa's questioning is born from his father's imperfect sacrifice.

vishisht.h: रामानुज की दृष्टि में वाजश्रवस् का यज्ञ भगवान् के प्रति समर्पण के अभाव में दोषपूर्ण है। सच्चा यज्ञ भगवान् को समर्पित होता है; स्वार्थ के लिए किया गया यज्ञ अधूरा है। नचिकेता का प्रश्न इसी अधूरेपन को पहचानता है।
vishisht.en: For Ramanuja, Vajashravasa's sacrifice is flawed because it lacks surrender to the Lord. True sacrifice is offered to the Lord; self-interested sacrifice is incomplete. Nachiketa's questioning recognises this incompleteness.
vishisht.ins: A sacrifice without surrender is merely a transaction. Nachiketa will show that the highest offering is oneself.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द 'उशन्' में मानव चेतना की मूल प्रवृत्ति देखते हैं — कामना। यज्ञ (sacrifice) उच्चतर चेतना की ओर जाने का साधन है, किन्तु कामना-प्रेरित यज्ञ अधूरा रहता है। नचिकेता — चेतना की अग्नि — इसी अधूरेपन से जन्म लेती है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo sees in 'uśan' the fundamental drive of human consciousness — desire. Sacrifice (yajña) is the means of ascending to higher consciousness, but desire-driven sacrifice remains incomplete. Nachiketa — the fire of consciousness — is born from this very incompleteness.
aurobindo.ins: The soul's aspiration (Nachiketa) emerges from the imperfection of the ego's offerings. The quest for truth begins where complacency ends.

dp.q: 🔍 What is the Vishvajit sacrifice and why is it significant?
dp.a: The Vishvajit ('all-conquering') sacrifice is a major Vedic rite in which the performer must give away all his possessions as dakṣiṇā (sacrificial fees) to the priests. It is the ultimate test of generosity — or so it appears. Vajashravasa performs it, but as the next verse will reveal, he gives away only old, barren, useless cattle. The sacrifice that demands 'everything' receives 'nothing of value.' This gap between the form and the spirit of the sacrifice is precisely what Nachiketa sees — and his seeing is the beginning of the Upanishad's teaching. The Vishvajit stands for any spiritual practice performed for show while withholding the genuine offering.

dp.q: 🔍 What does the name 'Nachiketa' mean?
dp.a: The etymology of Nachiketa is debated. The most common readings: (1) na + ciketa — 'not yet known/understood,' suggesting the boy embodies the question that has not yet been answered; (2) naci + ketas — 'the fire of inquiry/consciousness,' connecting him to the Nachiketa fire he will later learn from Yama; (3) the Taittiriya Brahmana derives it from √ci ('to arrange' the fire-altar). All three etymologies converge: Nachiketa is the embodiment of the question that burns — the fire of consciousness that seeks what lies beyond death. His very name is his destiny.

sk: तं ह कुमारं सन्तं दक्षिणासु नीयमानासु श्रद्धाविवेश | सोऽमन्यत ||
ro: taṁ · ha · kumāraṁ · santaṁ · dakṣiṇāsu · nīyamānāsu · śraddhā · āviveśa | so · amanyata ||
hi: जब दक्षिणा (यज्ञ-दान) की गाएँ ले जायी जा रही थीं, तब उस बालक (नचिकेता) में श्रद्धा ने प्रवेश किया। उसने सोचा —
en: As the gifts (cows given as sacrificial fees) were being led away, faith (śraddhā) entered the boy. He reflected —

ws.e: though still a boy — kumāra (youth) + santam (being); emphasises his young age
among the sacrificial gifts — locative plural feminine; the fees given to priests
being led away — present passive participle locative pl. of √nī ('to lead')
faith — not blind belief but the intuitive conviction that truth must be honoured
entered — perfect of ā+√viś ('to enter into'); śraddhā entered him like a divine force

gr: kumāraṁ santam — 'though being a boy': the concessive participle highlights that this insight came to a child, not a learned elder. śraddhā āviveśa — 'faith entered him': śraddhā is the subject, not Nachiketa — faith is portrayed as an active force that comes to the worthy, not something the seeker generates. amanyata — 'he reflected': middle voice of √man ('to think'); the reflection is internal, felt personally.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.1.2 — Śraddhā is the pivotal force of the entire Katha Upanishad. It is not mere belief but the deep conviction that truth must be lived. The boy sees worthless cows being given and is moved — not by anger but by faith in the sacred.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि श्रद्धा यहाँ सत्य के प्रति गहन निष्ठा है — कुमार ने देखा कि यज्ञ का स्वरूप दूषित है और उसे सत्य-मार्ग पर चलने की प्रेरणा मिली। 'आविवेश' — श्रद्धा बाहर से आयी, जैसे दैवी शक्ति।
advaita.en: Shankara reads śraddhā as deep conviction toward truth. The boy saw the sacrifice was corrupted and was moved to follow the path of truth. 'Āviveśa' — faith came from outside, like a divine force.
advaita.ins: Śraddhā is not manufactured; it descends upon the prepared soul. Nachiketa's purity made him the vessel for this descent.

vishisht.h: रामानुज श्रद्धा को भगवान् की कृपा का प्रारम्भिक स्पर्श मानते हैं। बालक की शुद्धता ने भगवान् की कृपा को आकृष्ट किया — और श्रद्धा के रूप में वह कृपा प्रकट हुई।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja reads śraddhā as the initial touch of the Lord's grace. The boy's purity attracted the Lord's grace — and it manifested as faith.
vishisht.ins: Grace finds the pure heart first. A child's innocence can be closer to the Lord than a learned man's scholarship.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द श्रद्धा को चेतना की आन्तरिक अग्नि मानते हैं — वह शक्ति जो सत्य को पहचानती है और असत्य को अस्वीकार करती है। नचिकेता में यह अग्नि जागी और उसने अपने पिता के कपटपूर्ण यज्ञ को देखा।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo reads śraddhā as the inner fire of consciousness — the power that recognises truth and rejects falsehood. This fire awakened in Nachiketa and he saw through his father's hollow sacrifice.
aurobindo.ins: Śraddhā is the soul's innate capacity for truth — it awakens in moments of crisis and demands authenticity.

dp.q: 🔍 Why is śraddhā described as 'entering' the boy, rather than arising in him?
dp.a: The Upanishad uses āviveśa — 'entered into' — with śraddhā as the grammatical subject and Nachiketa as the object. This is deliberately not 'Nachiketa developed faith' but 'faith entered Nachiketa.' The construction treats śraddhā as an independent force — a divine power that descends upon the worthy. In the Vedic worldview, śraddhā is not a psychological state the individual creates but a cosmic power (often personified as a goddess in the Ṛg Veda) that comes to those whose inner instrument is pure enough to receive it. The boy's innocence made him transparent; faith entered because there was no obstruction.

dp.q: 🔍 What did Nachiketa see that moved him so deeply?
dp.a: The next verse (mantra 3) tells us: he saw that the cows being given as dakṣiṇā were pītodakā (had drunk their last water), jagdhatṛṇā (had eaten their last grass), dugdhadohā (had given their last milk), and nirindriyāḥ (were devoid of vitality). His father was performing the ultimate sacrifice — giving away 'everything' — but actually giving away nothing of value. The boy saw the gap between the sacred form and the corrupt content. This moral clarity — seeing that a religious act can be spiritually empty — is what śraddhā produced in him.

sk: पीतोदका जग्धतृणा दुग्धदोहा निरिन्द्रियाः | अनन्दा नाम ते लोकास्तान् स गच्छति ता ददत् ||
ro: pītodakā · jagdhatṛṇā · dugdhadohā · nirindriyāḥ | ānandā · nāma · te · lokās · tān · sa · gacchati · tā · dadat ||
hi: इन गायों ने अन्तिम बार जल पी लिया है, अन्तिम बार घास खा ली है, अन्तिम बार दूध दे दिया है — ये निर्जीव हो चुकी हैं। जो ऐसी (निर्जीव वस्तुओं को) दान करता है, वह आनन्दरहित (अन्धकारमय) लोकों को जाता है।
en: These cows have drunk their last water, eaten their last grass, given their last milk — they are devoid of vigour. Joyless indeed are those worlds to which he goes who gives such as these.

ws.e: whose water is drunk up — bahuvrīhi compound: pīta (drunk) + udaka (water)
whose grass is eaten — jagdha (eaten, pp. of √jakṣ) + tṛṇa (grass)
whose milk is milked out — dugdha (milked) + doha (milking)
devoid of vigour/senses — nis (without) + indriya (vital power); barren and spent
joyless — an (without) + nanda (joy); or reading as 'ānandā' = blind/dark (from √and, 'to be blind')

gr: pītodakā jagdhatṛṇā dugdhadohā nirindriyāḥ — four bahuvrīhi compounds in succession, each describing an aspect of the cows' worthlessness: their water is consumed, grass eaten, milk exhausted, vitality spent. The stacking of compounds creates a devastating inventory. ānandā nāma te lokāḥ — 'joyless by name are those worlds': nāma ('by name, indeed') intensifies — those worlds are called joyless because that is their essential character.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.1.3 — The boy's moral insight: giving worthless things in a sacrifice meant to give everything is spiritual fraud. The four compounds (pītodakā, jagdhatṛṇā, dugdhadohā, nirindriyāḥ) are a devastating moral inventory — each word strips another layer of pretence from the gift.

advaita.h: शंकर इसे कर्मकाण्ड की सीमा के रूप में प्रस्तुत करते हैं: जो व्यक्ति अधूरे, दोषपूर्ण कर्म से फल चाहता है, वह 'अनन्द लोक' — आनन्दरहित स्थिति — को प्राप्त होता है। सच्चा दान सर्वस्व-समर्पण है, कूड़ा देना नहीं।
advaita.en: Shankara uses this to expose the limit of ritualism: one who seeks reward through flawed, incomplete ritual reaches 'ānanda loka' — a joyless state. True giving is total surrender, not discarding what is worthless.
advaita.ins: Spiritual practice that withholds the genuine offering — one's ego, one's attachments — while presenting the appearance of devotion leads to joyless worlds.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि बालक की इस अन्तर्दृष्टि में भगवान् की कृपा कार्य कर रही है। भगवान् के यज्ञ में सर्वश्रेष्ठ वस्तु अर्पित होनी चाहिए — निकृष्ट दान भगवान् का अपमान है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the Lord's grace is at work in the boy's insight. In the Lord's sacrifice, the best must be offered — giving the worst is an affront to the Lord.
vishisht.ins: The Lord accepts not the quantity but the quality of offering — and above all, the sincerity of the heart.

aurobindo.h: नचिकेता की दृष्टि में अरविन्द सत्य-चेतना (truth-consciousness) का प्रथम जागरण देखते हैं। बालक वह देख रहा है जो वयस्क नहीं देख पाते — कि आडम्बर और सत्य में अन्तर है।
aurobindo.en: In Nachiketa's vision, Aurobindo sees the first awakening of truth-consciousness. The boy sees what adults cannot — that appearance and truth are different.
aurobindo.ins: The child's seeing is uncorrupted by convention. When truth-consciousness awakens, the first thing it perceives is the gap between what is claimed and what is real.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does the Upanishad describe the cows in such physical detail?
dp.a: The four compounds — pītodakā, jagdhatṛṇā, dugdhadohā, nirindriyāḥ — form a devastating inventory of worthlessness. Each addresses a basic function: the cows can no longer drink (sustain themselves), eat (grow), give milk (nourish others), or exhibit vitality (be alive in any meaningful sense). The detail is not accidental — it forces the listener to see exactly what Vajashravasa is offering: not wealth but waste. The Upanishad is making a moral argument through biology: an offering that has already exhausted its value is not an offering at all. The physical detail becomes a spiritual metaphor — what are you truly giving in your spiritual practice? Your best, or your leftovers?

dp.q: 🔍 What are the 'joyless worlds' (ānandā lokāḥ)?
dp.a: The word ānandā can be read two ways: (1) an-nandā — 'without joy,' joyless; (2) from √and — 'blind, dark.' Both readings converge: the worlds earned by hollow sacrifice are dark and joyless. Shankara reads these as the realms of unfulfilled desire — where the sacrificer arrives expecting reward but finds nothing, because the sacrifice was empty. The warning is universal: any spiritual act performed without genuine offering leads to a state of spiritual bankruptcy. The 'worlds' are not just post-mortem destinations but states of consciousness — one can live in ānanda-loka right now, surrounded by the fruits of hollow effort.

sk: स होवाच पितरम् | तात कस्मै मां दास्यसीति | द्वितीयं तृतीयम् | तं होवाच मृत्यवे त्वा ददामीति ||
ro: sa · ha · uvāca · pitaram | tāta · kasmai · māṁ · dāsyasi · iti | dvitīyaṁ · tṛtīyam | taṁ · ha · uvāca · mṛtyave · tvā · dadāmi · iti ||
hi: उसने (नचिकेता ने) अपने पिता से कहा: 'पिताजी! आप मुझे किसको देंगे?' दूसरी बार, तीसरी बार (पूछा)। पिता ने (क्रोध में) कहा: 'मृत्यु को तुझे देता हूँ!'
en: He said to his father: 'Father, to whom will you give me?' A second time, a third time. The father replied: 'To Death I give you!'

ws.e: Father! — affectionate vocative; the tenderness of the address contrasts with the father's harsh reply
to whom — dative singular interrogative: 'for whose sake'
will you give — future 2nd sg. of √dā ('to give')
a second time, a third time — the threefold asking that pushes the father to the breaking point
to Death — dative singular of mṛtyu; Vajashravasa names Death as the recipient

gr: tāta kasmai māṁ dāsyasi — the boy's question is devastatingly simple: 'Father, to whom will you give me?' If the sacrifice requires giving everything, then the son too must be given. dvitīyaṁ tṛtīyam — the compressed narration ('a second time, a third time') shows Nachiketa's persistence and the father's growing irritation. mṛtyave tvā dadāmi — spoken in anger: the present tense 'dadāmi' (I give) makes it a performative utterance — the words enact the gift.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.1.4 — The verse that sets the entire Upanishad in motion. Nachiketa's question ('to whom will you give me?') is both the child's literal concern and the Upanishad's deepest question: what is the self, and to whom does it belong? The father's angry curse becomes the doorway to wisdom.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि नचिकेता का प्रश्न ('मुझे किसको दोगे?') दो स्तरों पर कार्य करता है: व्यावहारिक — यज्ञ में सब कुछ दिया जा रहा है तो पुत्र को भी देना चाहिए; और पारमार्थिक — 'मैं' (आत्मा) किसका है? पिता का क्रोधपूर्ण उत्तर 'मृत्यु को' अनजाने में सत्य बन जाता है — मृत्यु (यम) ही वह गुरु होगा जो आत्म-ज्ञान देगा।
advaita.en: Shankara says Nachiketa's question operates on two levels: practical — if everything is being given, the son should be included; and ultimate — to whom does the 'I' (Self) belong? The father's angry 'To Death!' unwittingly becomes truth — Death (Yama) will be the guru who imparts Self-knowledge.
advaita.ins: Sometimes the worst that can happen is what needs to happen. The curse becomes a blessing; the door to Death becomes the door to immortality.

vishisht.h: रामानुज के मत में नचिकेता का तीन बार पूछना भगवान् की प्रेरणा है — बालक को मृत्यु के पास भेजना भगवान् की योजना है ताकि परम ज्ञान प्रकट हो। पिता का क्रोध भगवान् की लीला का उपकरण बनता है।
vishisht.en: For Ramanuja, Nachiketa's triple asking is divinely prompted — sending the boy to Death is the Lord's plan so that supreme knowledge may be revealed. The father's anger becomes an instrument of divine play.
vishisht.ins: The Lord's plans unfold through human imperfection. Anger, accident, and crisis can be the vessels of grace.

aurobindo.h: अरविन्द इसे अन्तरात्मा (psychic being) के जागरण का क्षण मानते हैं। नचिकेता का प्रश्न 'मुझे किसको दोगे?' अहंकार का प्रश्न नहीं, अन्तरात्मा का प्रश्न है — 'यह जो मैं हूँ, यह किसके अधीन है? इसका सच्चा स्वामी कौन है?'
aurobindo.en: Aurobindo sees this as the awakening of the psychic being. Nachiketa's 'To whom will you give me?' is not the ego's question but the soul's — 'This that I am, to whom does it belong? Who is its true master?'
aurobindo.ins: The soul's question is always: 'To whom do I belong?' The answer — discovered through the encounter with Death — is: to the Immortal.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does Nachiketa ask three times?
dp.a: The triple asking has deep Vedic significance: three is the number of completeness (three worlds, three fires, three states of consciousness). Each asking intensifies the question: the first time is inquiry, the second is insistence, the third is spiritual demand. The father can dismiss once, ignore twice, but the third time forces a response. The triple asking also foreshadows the three boons Nachiketa will receive from Yama — three questions, three answers, three levels of knowledge. Narratively, the triple asking pushes the father past patience into anger — and the angry word ('To Death!') becomes the pivot of the entire story.

dp.q: 🔍 Is the father's 'To Death I give you' a curse or a blessing?
dp.a: It is both — and this duality is the Upanishad's first teaching about the relationship between death and truth. On the surface, it is a curse spoken in anger — the worst thing a father can say. In the story's logic, it becomes the greatest blessing — because it sends Nachiketa to the one teacher (Yama) who can answer the ultimate question. The Upanishad is showing that the encounter with mortality — which the ego experiences as the worst possible event — is actually the doorway to immortality. Every spiritual tradition echoes this: the 'dark night of the soul,' the 'descent into the underworld,' the 'death of the old self.' Vajashravasa's curse is the mechanism by which the soul finds its teacher.

sk: बहूनामेमि प्रथमो बहूनामेमि मध्यमः | किंस्विद्यमस्य कर्तव्यं यन्मयाद्य करिष्यति ||
ro: bahūnām · emi · prathamo · bahūnām · emi · madhyamaḥ | kiṁsvid · yamasya · kartavyaṁ · yan · mayā · adya · kariṣyati ||
hi: नचिकेता ने सोचा: 'अनेक शिष्यों में मैं प्रथम श्रेणी का हूँ, अनेकों में मध्यम श्रेणी का (कदापि अधम नहीं)। यम का कौन-सा कार्य है जो वे आज मेरे द्वारा सम्पन्न करेंगे?'
en: Nachiketa reflected: 'Among many I go as the first; among many I go as middling (never the worst). What purpose of Yama's will he accomplish through me today?'

ws.e: among many — genitive plural: 'of many' (students/souls)
I go — present 1st sg. of √i ('to go'); 'I rank, I proceed'
first, foremost — nominative adjective: 'as the best'
middling, median — 'never the worst'
what indeed? — interrogative particle expressing genuine wondering
work to be done, purpose — gerundive of √kṛ; 'what must be done'

gr: bahūnām emi prathamaḥ — 'among many I go first': the boy assesses his own worth — he is not an inferior student. bahūnām emi madhyamaḥ — 'among many, middling': at worst, he is in the middle — never the lowest. This is not boasting but honest self-assessment before a daunting journey. kiṁsvid yamasya kartavyam — 'what purpose of Yama?' — the question shifts from self-assessment to cosmic purpose: what will Death do with me?
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.1.5 — Nachiketa's inner monologue as he prepares to go to Yama. The verse reveals remarkable composure: instead of panic, the boy calmly assesses his worth and wonders what purpose Death might have for him. This is śraddhā in action — faith transmuted into courage.

advaita.h: शंकर इसे विवेक (discrimination) का लक्षण बताते हैं: बालक भयभीत नहीं है, वह विचार कर रहा है। 'मैं प्रथम या मध्यम हूँ' — अर्थात् मेरा जीवन व्यर्थ नहीं है, मृत्यु मुझसे कुछ सीखा सकती है या कोई उद्देश्य पूरा कर सकती है।
advaita.en: Shankara reads this as the sign of viveka (discrimination): the boy is not afraid but reflective. 'I am first or middling' — my life has value; Death can teach me something or accomplish some purpose through me.
advaita.ins: The prepared soul meets death not with terror but with inquiry — 'What can this experience teach me?'

vishisht.h: नचिकेता का आत्म-मूल्यांकन विनम्रता और आत्मविश्वास का संयोग है। वह अपने को सर्वश्रेष्ठ नहीं कहता, किन्तु निकृष्ट भी नहीं — यही शरणागति के योग्य जीव का लक्षण है।
vishisht.en: Nachiketa's self-assessment blends humility and confidence. He does not claim to be the best but refuses to be the worst — this is the mark of a soul worthy of surrender.
vishisht.ins: The soul approaching the Lord needs both humility (I am not the greatest) and dignity (I am not worthless). Both are needed for genuine surrender.

aurobindo.h: अरविन्द इसे अन्तरात्मा की आत्म-जागरूकता मानते हैं। नचिकेता अपने स्तर को जानता है — और जानता है कि मृत्यु के साथ भेंट में कोई गहरा उद्देश्य अवश्य है। यह चेतना का वह स्तर है जो दैवी योजना को सहज रूप से अनुभव करता है।
aurobindo.en: Aurobindo reads this as the psychic being's self-awareness. Nachiketa knows his level — and senses that the encounter with Death must serve a deeper purpose. This is the level of consciousness that intuitively feels the divine plan.
aurobindo.ins: The soul that senses purpose in adversity is already aligned with the Transcendent's intention.

dp.q: 🔍 What does Nachiketa's self-assessment reveal about his character?
dp.a: In two brief phrases — 'Among many I go first; among many I go middling' — Nachiketa reveals a character rare in spiritual literature. He is neither arrogant ('I am the best') nor falsely humble ('I am nothing'). He makes an honest, grounded assessment: sometimes he excels, sometimes he is average, but he is never the worst. This balance of self-knowledge is what the Upanishad considers the prerequisite for meeting Death. A soul consumed by pride would demand special treatment; a soul crushed by self-doubt would be paralysed. Nachiketa's balanced self-regard allows him to face Yama with the composure needed to ask — and receive — the ultimate teaching.

dp.q: 🔍 What does 'What purpose of Yama will he accomplish through me?' mean?
dp.a: The question 'kiṁsvid yamasya kartavyam' is extraordinary for a child facing death. Instead of asking 'What will happen to me?' Nachiketa asks 'What will Yama accomplish through me?' The focus shifts from self-concern to cosmic purpose. The boy intuites that even Death has a dharma — a function to fulfill — and that his own journey to Yama's house might serve that function. In the story, this intuition proves correct: Nachiketa's visit gives Yama the opportunity to teach the highest wisdom. The boy does not know this yet, but his question shows the orientation of a soul aligned with larger purposes.

sk: अनुपश्य यथा पूर्वे प्रतिपश्य तथापरे | सस्यमिव मर्त्यः पच्यते सस्यमिवाजायते पुनः ||
ro: anupaśya · yathā · pūrve · pratipaśya · tathā · apare | sasyam · iva · martyaḥ · pacyate · sasyam · iva · ājāyate · punaḥ ||
hi: देखो, पूर्वजों ने कैसा किया; देखो, परवर्ती कैसा करेंगे। मनुष्य अन्न (फसल) की तरह पकता है और अन्न की तरह पुनः उत्पन्न होता है।
en: Look back at how the ancients acted; look forward at how later ones will act. A mortal ripens like grain, and like grain is born again.

ws.e: look back — imperative of anu+√paś ('to look along, look back')
look forward — imperative of prati+√paś ('to look toward, anticipate')
like grain — sasyam (grain, harvest); iva (like); the crop metaphor
ripens — passive of √pac ('to cook, ripen'); maturation leading to death
is born again — passive of ā+√jan ('to be born'); the cycle of rebirth

gr: anupaśya... pratipaśya — two imperatives creating a temporal sweep: look back (at ancestors), look forward (at descendants). The double perspective places the individual life in the flow of generations. sasyam iva pacyate — 'ripens like grain': the agricultural metaphor is profound — grain ripens, is cut, and from its seed, new grain grows. sasyam iva ājāyate punaḥ — 'like grain is born again': the cycle of birth-death-rebirth is presented not as a doctrine but as an observable fact of nature.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.1.6 — Nachiketa consoles himself (or his father) with the reflection on mortality: all beings die and are reborn, like the agricultural cycle. This verse introduces the theme of the entire Katha Upanishad: what lies beyond this cycle?

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि यह श्लोक नचिकेता का अपने पिता को (या स्वयं को) आश्वासन है: मृत्यु सार्वभौमिक है, पूर्वज भी मरे, भावी पीढ़ियाँ भी मरेंगी। किन्तु इस सांत्वना के भीतर बड़ा प्रश्न छिपा है — क्या इस चक्र से परे कुछ है?
advaita.en: Shankara reads this as Nachiketa's consolation to his father (or himself): death is universal; ancestors died, future generations will die. But within this consolation lies the greater question — is there anything beyond this cycle?
advaita.ins: Accepting mortality is the first step; transcending it is the journey of the Katha Upanishad.

vishisht.h: रामानुज इस चक्र को भगवान् की सृष्टि-लीला का अंश मानते हैं। जन्म-मृत्यु-पुनर्जन्म भगवान् की व्यवस्था है — किन्तु भक्त इस चक्र से परे भगवान् के नित्य धाम को प्राप्त करता है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja sees the cycle as part of the Lord's creative play. Birth-death-rebirth is the Lord's arrangement — but the devotee transcends this cycle to reach the Lord's eternal abode.
vishisht.ins: The grain-cycle is not the soul's destiny — it is the condition from which the Lord's grace liberates.

aurobindo.h: अरविन्द इस श्लोक में विकासवाद (evolution) का बीज देखते हैं: चेतना अन्न की तरह बार-बार जन्म लेती है — प्रत्येक जन्म में कुछ और परिपक्व होती है, जब तक वह मृत्यु के चक्र से ऊपर नहीं उठ जाती।
aurobindo.en: Aurobindo sees the seed of evolution in this verse: consciousness is born again and again like grain — each birth ripening it further, until it rises above the death-cycle.
aurobindo.ins: Rebirth is not pointless repetition but progressive evolution. Each life adds something; the soul is gradually ripening toward a transformation that transcends the cycle entirely.

dp.q: 🔍 Why the grain metaphor for human mortality?
dp.a: The metaphor sasyam iva (like grain) works on multiple levels. Grain ripens (pacyate — literally 'cooks' in the sun), is harvested (cut down at its peak), and from its seed grows again. This is the most intimate image available to a Vedic audience — every family grew grain, every harvest enacted the death-and-rebirth cycle. But the metaphor contains its own transcendence: grain serves a purpose beyond its own cycle — it feeds and sustains others. The implication: human life too serves a purpose beyond its own birth-death cycle. What that purpose is — that is the question Nachiketa will ask Yama.

dp.q: 🔍 Is this verse about reincarnation?
dp.a: The phrase 'ājāyate punaḥ' (is born again) is one of the earliest Upanishadic references to rebirth. But the verse does not present reincarnation as a philosophical doctrine — it presents it as an observation from nature. Grain dies and is reborn; so too is the mortal. The Katha Upanishad will go beyond this observation to ask: what is reborn? Is it the same self? Is there something that does not die? Nachiketa's question to Yama in mantra 20 — 'When a man dies, does he exist or not?' — is the deepest form of this inquiry. This verse sets up the question; the answer will take the rest of the Upanishad.

sk: वैश्वानरः प्रविशत्यतिथिर्ब्राह्मणो गृहान् | तस्यैतां शान्तिं कुर्वन्ति हर वैवस्वतोदकम् ||
ro: vaiśvānaraḥ · praviśati · atithir · brāhmaṇo · gṛhān | tasyai · etāṁ · śāntiṁ · kurvanti · hara · vaivasvata · udakam ||
hi: वैश्वानर (अग्नि) की भाँति ब्राह्मण अतिथि गृह में प्रवेश करता है। उसकी शान्ति (तृप्ति) के लिए लोग यह करते हैं — हे वैवस्वत (यमराज), जल लाइए!
en: Like Vaishvanara (fire), a Brahmin guest enters a house. People make this offering of peace to him — Bring water, O son of Vivasvat (Yama)!

ws.e: Vaishvanara — the universal fire; epithet of Agni as the fire in all beings
guest — literally 'without a fixed date (a-tithi)'; one who arrives unannounced
peace-offering, propitiation — from √śam ('to be calm'); the hospitality that appeases the guest's fire
O son of Vivasvat — patronymic of Yama; Vivasvat = the Sun
water — the first offering to an arriving guest; a Vedic protocol

gr: vaiśvānaraḥ praviśati — 'like Vaishvanara he enters': the simile of fire for a guest is both honorific and cautionary — an unhonoured guest burns the host's merit like uncontained fire. atithir brāhmaṇaḥ — 'a Brahmin guest': the highest category of guest in Vedic society. hara vaivasvata udakam — a direct command within the verse: 'Bring water, O Yama!' This is spoken by Yama's attendants (or by the narrative voice) reminding Yama of his host's duty. Nachiketa waited three nights without food — Yama must now make amends.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.1.7 — The verse transitions from Nachiketa's reflections to his arrival at Yama's house. A Brahmin guest is like fire — fail to honour him and he consumes your merit. This verse establishes why Yama owes Nachiketa three boons.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि अतिथि-धर्म वैदिक संस्कृति का मूल है। ब्राह्मण अतिथि अग्नि-स्वरूप है — उसकी उपेक्षा सब पुण्य नष्ट करती है। यम स्वयं इस धर्म से बँधा है — मृत्यु भी अतिथि-धर्म का उल्लंघन नहीं कर सकती।
advaita.en: Shankara says atithi-dharma (hospitality) is foundational to Vedic culture. The Brahmin guest is fire incarnate — neglecting him destroys all merit. Even Yama is bound by this dharma — Death itself cannot violate hospitality.
advaita.ins: The universe operates on dharma. Even the Lord of Death must honour the guest who comes to his door.

vishisht.h: रामानुज इसे भगवान् की व्यवस्था मानते हैं: अतिथि-सेवा भगवत्-सेवा है। यम ने अतिथि-धर्म का पालन किया — यह दर्शाता है कि धर्म भगवान् से ऊपर नहीं, किन्तु भगवान् धर्म के माध्यम से कार्य करते हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja sees this as the Lord's arrangement: serving the guest is serving the Lord. Yama honoured his guest-duty — showing that dharma is not above the Lord but the Lord works through dharma.
vishisht.ins: Every act of hospitality is an act of worship. The guest carries the divine fire.

aurobindo.h: अरविन्द अतिथि को चेतना की उस उच्चतर शक्ति के रूप में देखते हैं जो अप्रत्याशित रूप से आती है और सब कुछ बदल देती है। नचिकेता यम के घर में 'अतिथि' है — वह चेतना की अग्नि है जो मृत्यु के क्षेत्र में प्रवेश करती है।
aurobindo.en: Aurobindo reads the guest as the higher power of consciousness that arrives unexpectedly and changes everything. Nachiketa is the 'guest' in Yama's house — the fire of consciousness entering the domain of Death.
aurobindo.ins: When the aspiring soul enters the realm of death, death itself must respond — not with destruction but with teaching.

dp.q: 🔍 Why is a guest compared to fire (Vaishvanara)?
dp.a: The comparison of a guest to Vaishvanara (universal fire) operates on two levels. Positive: a guest carries divine fire — his presence purifies and blesses the household. Offering him food and water is like offering oblations into a sacred fire. Cautionary: fire unhonoured becomes destructive. A neglected guest 'burns' the host's accumulated merit — hope (āśā), expectation (pratīkṣā), the fruit of association (saṅgata), pleasant speech (sūnṛtā), sacrificial merit (iṣṭāpūrta), sons and cattle. The next verse (mantra 8) will list exactly what is destroyed. The metaphor is thus both an invitation and a warning — hospitality is sacred because the guest embodies the sacred fire.

dp.q: 🔍 Why is Yama called 'Vaivasvata' (son of the Sun)?
dp.a: Vaivasvata — patronymic of Yama, meaning 'descendant of Vivasvat (the Sun)' — connects Death to the solar principle. In Vedic cosmology, the Sun is the source of light, life, and truth; Yama, as the Sun's son, is not darkness but the other face of light. Death is not the opposite of life but the guardian of life's boundaries. This solar lineage also explains why Yama can teach the highest truth: he is not a demon or enemy but a cosmic functionary of the solar order — Ṛta itself. The address 'O Vaivasvata' simultaneously acknowledges Yama's authority (as lord of the dead) and his luminous lineage (as son of the Sun).

sk: आशाप्रतीक्षे संगतं सूनृतां चेष्टापूर्ते पुत्रपशूंश्च सर्वान् | एतद्वृङ्क्ते पुरुषस्याल्पमेधसो यस्यानश्नन्वसति ब्राह्मणो गृहे ||
ro: āśā · pratīkṣe · saṅgataṁ · sūnṛtāṁ · ca · iṣṭāpūrte · putra · paśūṁś · ca · sarvān | etad · vṛṅkte · puruṣasya · alpamedhasaḥ · yasya · anaśnan · vasati · brāhmaṇo · gṛhe ||
hi: आशा और अपेक्षा, संगति का फल, मधुर वाणी का पुण्य, इष्ट (यज्ञ) और पूर्त (लोकहित कर्म) का फल, पुत्र और पशु — यह सब नष्ट हो जाता है उस अल्पबुद्धि व्यक्ति का, जिसके घर में ब्राह्मण अतिथि बिना भोजन के रहता है।
en: Hope and expectation, the fruit of association, pleasant speech, the merit of sacrifices and charitable works, sons and cattle — all this is destroyed for the man of small understanding in whose house a Brahmin guest stays without food.

ws.e: hope — the expectation of future good; destroyed by inhospitality
expectation — the anticipation of results from past actions

ws.h: यज्ञ और लोकहित कर्मों का फल
ws.e: merit of sacrifices (iṣṭa) and charitable works (pūrta) — the two categories of Vedic merit

ws.h: नष्ट कर देता है, छीन लेता है
ws.e: destroys, tears away — present middle of √vṛj or √vraśc ('to cut, uproot')
of small understanding — alpa (small) + medhas (wisdom, intelligence)

gr: āśā pratīkṣe saṅgataṁ sūnṛtāṁ ca iṣṭāpūrte putra-paśūṁś ca sarvān — a comprehensive inventory of everything a householder values: seven categories spanning hope, social relations, speech-merit, ritual-merit, and progeny. etad vṛṅkte — 'this is torn away': the middle voice suggests the merit self-destructs. alpamedhasaḥ — 'of small understanding': the one who neglects a guest is not evil but foolish — alpa-medhas, lacking wisdom.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.1.8 — The verse specifies the sevenfold destruction that befalls a host who neglects a Brahmin guest. This is not a threat but a description of spiritual consequence — inhospitality reverses the karmic current.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि यह श्लोक मृत्यु (यम) को नचिकेता के प्रति अपने कर्तव्य का बोध कराता है। तीन रातें बिना भोजन — यम का सब पुण्य नष्ट हो रहा है। तीन वरदान इसी क्षति की भरपाई हैं।
advaita.en: Shankara says this verse reminds Death (Yama) of his obligation. Three nights without food — Yama's merit is being destroyed. The three boons compensate for this loss.
advaita.ins: Even the lord of dharma is subject to dharma. No being is above the law of hospitality.

vishisht.h: रामानुज इस श्लोक में भगवान् की व्यवस्था देखते हैं: अतिथि-सेवा का उल्लंघन सब धार्मिक संचय को नष्ट करता है। यह इसलिए कि अतिथि में भगवान् निवास करते हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja sees the Lord's law here: violating guest-service destroys all religious accumulation — because the Lord dwells in the guest.
vishisht.ins: Every being is a dwelling of the Lord. Neglecting any being is neglecting the Lord Himself.

aurobindo.h: अरविन्द इसे चेतना के नियम के रूप में पढ़ते हैं: जब उच्चतर शक्ति (अतिथि/चेतना की अग्नि) उपेक्षित होती है, तब निम्न स्तर का सब संचय विघटित हो जाता है। आध्यात्मिक अवसर की उपेक्षा सबसे बड़ी हानि है।
aurobindo.en: Aurobindo reads this as a law of consciousness: when a higher power (the guest / fire of consciousness) is neglected, all accumulation at the lower level disintegrates. Neglecting a spiritual opportunity is the greatest loss.
aurobindo.ins: When the call of the higher consciousness arrives and is ignored, the fruits of all prior effort are undone.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does the Upanishad list exactly seven things that are destroyed?
dp.a: The seven items — hope, expectation, association's fruit, pleasant speech, sacrificial merit, charitable merit, sons and cattle — cover the complete field of a Vedic householder's life. They span three domains: temporal (hope, expectation), social (association, speech), and spiritual (iṣṭa-pūrta, progeny). The comprehensive listing shows that inhospitality does not cause partial damage — it causes total destruction. The neglected guest-fire burns through every category of accumulated good. This totality makes Yama's situation urgent: three nights of a hungry Brahmin guest means three-fold total destruction of merit.

dp.q: 🔍 How does this verse set up the three boons?
dp.a: Nachiketa waited three nights without food in Yama's house. The sevenfold destruction listed here means Yama has suffered catastrophic karmic loss. The three boons are not a generous gift but a necessary restitution — one boon per night of neglect. This is significant: the boons are not Yama's choice but his obligation. He must offer them. The framework of obligation ensures that even when Nachiketa asks the most difficult question (the third boon — what happens after death), Yama cannot refuse. The hospitality-debt becomes the lever by which the deepest teaching is extracted from Death.

sk: तिस्रो रात्रीर्यदवात्सीर्गृहे मेऽनश्नन्ब्रह्मन्नतिथिर्नमस्यः | नमस्तेऽस्तु ब्रह्मन्स्वस्ति मेऽस्तु तस्मात्प्रति त्रीन्वरान्वृणीष्व ||
ro: tisro · rātrīr · yad · avātsīr · gṛhe · me · anaśnan · brahman · atithir · namasyaḥ | namas · te · astu · brahman · svasti · me · astu · tasmāt · prati · trīn · varān · vṛṇīṣva ||
hi: यम बोले: 'हे ब्राह्मण! तुम तीन रातें मेरे घर में बिना भोजन के रहे — तुम नमस्य (वन्दनीय) अतिथि हो। तुम्हें नमस्कार! हे ब्राह्मण, मेरा कल्याण हो। इसलिए तीन वरदान माँगो।'
en: Yama said: 'Three nights you stayed in my house without eating, O Brahmin, O worthy guest. Salutations to you! O Brahmin, may it be well with me. Therefore choose three boons.'

ws.e: three nights — accusative pl.; the duration of Nachiketa's fast at Yama's door
you stayed — aorist 2nd sg. of √vas ('to dwell, stay')
without eating — present participle negative of √aś ('to eat')
worthy of reverence — gerundive of √nam ('to bow'); 'one who must be bowed to'
choose boons — varān (acc. pl. of vara, 'boon') + vṛṇīṣva (imperative middle of √vṛ, 'to choose')

gr: tisro rātrīḥ — three nights: each night corresponds to one boon. anaśnan brahman atithir namasyaḥ — three vocatives/descriptions packed together: 'without eating, O Brahmin, a guest worthy of reverence.' namas te astu... svasti me astu — two parallel wishes: 'salutations to you; may it be well with me.' The second wish reveals Yama's genuine concern — he fears the karmic consequences of neglecting a guest. trīn varān vṛṇīṣva — 'choose three boons': the number matches the three nights; the imperative middle voice gives Nachiketa full choice.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.1.9 — Yama's formal offer of three boons. Death bows to Nachiketa — a reversal of the usual power dynamic. The lord of death becomes the servant of dharma, obligated by hospitality to grant whatever the boy asks.

advaita.h: शंकर बताते हैं कि 'स्वस्ति मेऽस्तु' (मेरा कल्याण हो) यम की चिन्ता दर्शाता है — तीन रातें अतिथि भूखा रहा, यम का पुण्य-संचय खतरे में है। तीन वरदान आवश्यकता हैं, उदारता नहीं।
advaita.en: Shankara notes 'svasti me astu' (may it be well with me) reveals Yama's concern — three nights of a hungry guest endangers his accumulated merit. The three boons are necessity, not generosity.
advaita.ins: Even Death needs the guest's forgiveness. Dharma operates at every level of existence — no being is exempt.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि यम का नचिकेता को 'ब्रह्मन्' (ब्राह्मण) कहकर सम्बोधित करना दर्शाता है कि यम इस बालक में दिव्यता को पहचानता है। भगवान् ने इस बालक को विशेष कृपा से भेजा है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says Yama's addressing Nachiketa as 'brahman' (O Brahmin) shows Death recognises the divinity in this boy. The Lord has sent this child with special grace.
vishisht.ins: When the Lord's chosen soul arrives, even Death recognises and bows.

aurobindo.h: अरविन्द में यम चेतना की उस शक्ति का प्रतीक है जो सीमा और अन्त को नियन्त्रित करती है। जब अभीप्सा (aspiration) की अग्नि (नचिकेता) तीन रातें (तीन अवस्थाओं — जागृत, स्वप्न, सुषुप्ति — का प्रतीक) पार करके मृत्यु के समक्ष खड़ी होती है, तब मृत्यु को झुकना पड़ता है।
aurobindo.en: In Aurobindo, Yama symbolises the power of consciousness that governs limit and cessation. When the fire of aspiration (Nachiketa) crosses three nights (symbolising the three states of waking, dream, and deep sleep) and stands before Death, Death must bow.
aurobindo.ins: The aspiring soul that passes through all three states of ordinary consciousness and arrives at the threshold of the Beyond compels even the guardian of that threshold to teach.

dp.q: 🔍 Why three nights and three boons?
dp.a: The number three pervades the Katha Upanishad and Vedic thought generally. Three nights represent a complete temporal cycle (past, present, future; or the three states of waking, dream, and deep sleep). Three boons map a hierarchy of human aspiration: the first boon (family harmony) addresses the social self; the second (the Nachiketa fire) addresses the ritual/cosmic self; the third (what happens after death) addresses the ultimate self. The structure moves from the outermost concern (will my father forgive me?) to the innermost (does the self survive death?). Each boon peels away a layer of the human condition until only the final, irreducible question remains.

dp.q: 🔍 What does it mean that Death (Yama) bows to Nachiketa?
dp.a: The reversal is precise and deliberate: the lord of death says 'namas te' (salutations to you) and 'svasti me astu' (may it be well with me) — Death is worried about its own welfare before the Brahmin guest. This is the Upanishad's first structural teaching: death is not the ultimate power. The ultimate power is dharma — the cosmic order that even Death must obey. Nachiketa, by his purity and his father's word, has entered Death's domain not as a victim but as a guest who carries the sacred fire. Death bows not to the boy personally but to the dharma he embodies. This reversal is the story's promise: by the end, Death will not merely bow but will teach — the secret of immortality.

sk: शान्तसंकल्पः सुमना यथा स्याद्वीतमन्युर्गौतमो माभि मृत्यो | त्वत्प्रसृष्टं माभिवदेत्प्रतीत एतत्त्रयाणां प्रथमं वरं वृणे ||
ro: śānta·saṁkalpaḥ · sumanā · yathā · syād · vīta·manyur · gautamo · mā · abhi · mṛtyo | tvat·prasṛṣṭaṁ · mā · abhivadet · pratīta · etat · trayāṇāṁ · prathamaṁ · varaṁ · vṛṇe ||
hi: नचिकेता ने कहा: 'हे मृत्यो! मेरे पिता गौतम शान्तचित्त, प्रसन्नमना और क्रोधरहित हों। आपसे छोड़ा हुआ मुझे पहचानकर स्नेहपूर्वक बोलें। तीनों वरों में यह पहला वर मैं माँगता हूँ।'
en: 'May Gautama (my father) be calm-minded, cheerful, free from anger toward me, O Death. May he recognise me when released by you and speak to me with love. This is the first of the three boons I choose.'

ws.e: calm-minded — śānta (peaceful) + saṁkalpa (intention, mind)
cheerful, well-disposed — su (good) + manas (mind)
free from anger — vīta (gone, departed) + manyu (anger, wrath)
Gautama — the father's clan name (gotra)
released by you — tvat (from you) + prasṛṣṭa (sent forth, released)
recognising, confident — past participle of prati+√i ('to recognise, approach with confidence')

gr: śānta-saṁkalpaḥ su-manāḥ vīta-manyuḥ — three compounds describing the desired state of the father: calm intention, good mind, anger departed. mā abhi mṛtyo — 'toward me, O Death': Nachiketa addresses Death directly while asking about his father — the intimacy is striking. prathamaṁ varaṁ vṛṇe — 'I choose the first boon': the formal, deliberate language shows Nachiketa's composure.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.1.10 — The first boon is entirely about human relationships — Nachiketa wants his father's love restored. Before seeking cosmic or metaphysical knowledge, the boy secures the human bond. This reveals the Upanishad's understanding: spiritual aspiration does not negate human affection.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि प्रथम वरदान लौकिक है — पारिवारिक सम्बन्ध की शान्ति। यह दर्शाता है कि ज्ञान-मार्ग पारिवारिक कर्तव्य की उपेक्षा नहीं करता, बल्कि पहले उसे सुलझाता है और फिर उच्चतर ज्ञान की ओर बढ़ता है।
advaita.en: Shankara says the first boon is worldly — family reconciliation. This shows the path of knowledge does not neglect family duty; it first resolves that and then proceeds to higher knowledge.
advaita.ins: Settle your human obligations before seeking the ultimate. The spiritual path does not require abandoning love — it requires completing it.

vishisht.h: रामानुज नचिकेता के प्रथम वरदान में पुत्र-धर्म और पितृ-भक्ति देखते हैं। बालक को अपने लिए कुछ नहीं चाहिए — वह पहले अपने पिता की शान्ति चाहता है। यह सच्ची भक्ति की पूर्व-शर्त है: मानवीय सम्बन्धों की पवित्रता।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja sees in the first boon filial duty and devotion to the father. The boy wants nothing for himself — he first wants his father's peace. This is the prerequisite for true devotion: the sanctity of human relationships.
vishisht.ins: One who cannot love the father one has seen cannot love the Lord one has not seen. Begin with human love.

aurobindo.h: अरविन्द प्रथम वरदान को चेतना की पहली आवश्यकता मानते हैं: बाह्य जीवन में शान्ति। जब तक बाहरी सम्बन्ध अशान्त हैं, तब तक भीतरी अन्वेषण असम्भव है। नचिकेता पहले बाह्य शान्ति स्थापित करता है, फिर भीतर जाता है।
aurobindo.en: Aurobindo reads the first boon as consciousness's primary need: peace in outer life. While external relationships are disturbed, inner inquiry is impossible. Nachiketa first establishes outer peace, then turns inward.
aurobindo.ins: The spiritual journey requires a settled base. Resolve outer conflicts first — not as an end but as the foundation for deeper work.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does Nachiketa ask about his father first, before anything cosmic?
dp.a: This is one of the most humanly touching moments in all the Upanishads. Nachiketa is standing before Death itself, granted three wishes — and his first thought is: let my father not be angry at me. The boy does not ask for personal gain, cosmic power, or even spiritual knowledge first. He asks for reconciliation. This reveals the Upanishad's understanding of spiritual hierarchy: the foundation of all knowledge is right relationship. A seeker carrying unresolved human pain cannot receive the highest teaching — the pain would distort the reception. Nachiketa clears the emotional ground before building the spiritual edifice.

dp.q: 🔍 What do the three descriptors (śānta-saṁkalpa, su-manā, vīta-manyu) tell us?
dp.a: Nachiketa asks for three specific states in his father: śānta-saṁkalpa (calm intention — the deep mind at rest), su-manā (good mind, cheerful — the emotional surface at peace), and vīta-manyu (anger departed — the reactive layer dissolved). These three map the layers of the mind: intention (saṁkalpa), mood (manas), and passion (manyu). Nachiketa wants healing at all three levels — not just outward civility but deep inner peace in his father. This precision shows the boy's psychological maturity: he knows that surface politeness without inner calm is hollow, just as his father's sacrifice was hollow.

sk: यथा पुरस्ताद्भविता प्रतीत औद्दालकिरारुणिर्मत्प्रसृष्टः | सुखं रात्रीः शयिता वीतमन्युः त्वां ददृशिवान्मृत्युमुखात्प्रमुक्तम् ||
ro: yathā · purastād · bhavitā · pratīta · auddālakir · āruṇir · mat·prasṛṣṭaḥ | sukhaṁ · rātrīḥ · śayitā · vīta·manyuḥ · tvāṁ · dadṛśivān · mṛtyu·mukhāt · pramuktam ||
hi: यम बोले: 'जैसा पहले था, वैसा ही तेरा पिता औद्दालकि आरुणि मेरी अनुमति से प्रसन्न होगा। वह क्रोधरहित होकर रात्रियों में सुखपूर्वक सोयेगा — तुझे मृत्यु के मुख से मुक्त हुआ देखकर।'
en: Yama said: 'As before, your father Auddalaki Aruni, released by me, will be at peace. He will sleep happily through the nights, free from anger, having seen you freed from the jaws of Death.'

ws.e: as before — adverb: the father will return to his prior affectionate state
son of Uddalaka Aruni — the father's full patronymic lineage
released by me — mat (from me) + prasṛṣṭa (sent forth, permitted)
having seen — perfect active participle of √dṛś ('to see'); the father will have the experience of seeing

ws.h: मृत्यु के मुख से छूटा हुआ
ws.e: freed from the mouth of Death — a vivid image: Nachiketa was 'in Death's jaws' and is now released

gr: auddālakir āruṇiḥ — double patronymic: 'Auddalaki' (descendant of Uddalaka) and 'Aruni' (descendant of Aruna). This formal naming grants the father dignity even in his error. mṛtyumukhāt pramuktam — 'freed from Death's mouth': the most vivid phrase — Nachiketa was literally inside Death's domain, and Yama releases him. sukhaṁ rātrīḥ śayitā — 'will sleep happily through the nights': the specific mention of restful sleep shows Yama understands that the father's guilt has been destroying his rest.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.1.11 — Yama grants the first boon generously. The father will be restored to his original loving state — anger dissolved, guilt removed, sleep restored. The phrase 'freed from the mouth of Death' is both literal and symbolic.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि प्रथम वरदान शीघ्रता से दिया गया — यम को इसमें कोई कठिनाई नहीं। लौकिक समस्याओं का समाधान मृत्यु के लिए सरल है। कठिनाई तीसरे वरदान में आयेगी — जहाँ नचिकेता मृत्यु से परे का प्रश्न पूछेगा।
advaita.en: Shankara notes the first boon is granted swiftly — Yama finds no difficulty. Worldly problems are easy for Death. The difficulty will come with the third boon — where Nachiketa will ask what lies beyond death.
advaita.ins: Death can solve worldly problems effortlessly. It is the question about death itself that Death struggles to answer.

vishisht.h: यम की उदारता भगवान् की कृपा का प्रतिबिम्ब है। भगवान् सबसे पहले भक्त के लौकिक दुःख दूर करते हैं — फिर उसे उच्चतर ज्ञान की ओर ले जाते हैं।
vishisht.en: Yama's generosity reflects the Lord's grace. The Lord first removes the devotee's worldly suffering — then leads to higher knowledge.
vishisht.ins: Grace operates in stages: first healing, then teaching, then liberation.

aurobindo.h: अरविन्द कहते हैं कि बाह्य सम्बन्धों की शान्ति आन्तरिक अन्वेषण की पूर्वशर्त है। यम इसे तुरन्त प्रदान करता है क्योंकि यह चेतना के निम्न स्तर का कार्य है — सच्ची चुनौती आगे है।
aurobindo.en: Aurobindo says peace in outer relationships is the precondition for inner exploration. Yama grants it instantly because this operates at a lower level of consciousness — the real challenge lies ahead.
aurobindo.ins: The outer life must be settled before the inner journey can truly begin.

dp.q: 🔍 What does 'freed from the mouth of Death' (mṛtyumukhāt pramuktam) mean?
dp.a: The phrase mṛtyu-mukhāt pramuktam — 'released from Death's mouth' — is extraordinarily vivid. It imagines Death as a creature that has swallowed Nachiketa, and now disgorges him. This is not mere metaphor — in the story, Nachiketa has literally been 'given to Death' by his father and has spent three days in Yama's domain. The release is physical and spiritual: the boy returns from death's realm to the living world. But the phrase also foreshadows the Upanishad's ultimate teaching: the Self was never truly 'in Death's mouth' — the Self is immortal. The release from Death's jaws is not an escape but a recognition that Death never truly held the Self at all.

dp.q: 🔍 Why is restful sleep (sukhaṁ rātrīḥ śayitā) specifically mentioned?
dp.a: Yama promises that the father will 'sleep happily through the nights' — a strikingly specific detail. This implies the father has been unable to sleep since sending his son to Death. Guilt, anger, and grief have destroyed his rest. In Vedic and Upanishadic psychology, sleep is the barometer of inner peace — one who cannot sleep is at war with himself. Yama's promise addresses the deepest consequence of the father's curse: not just anger but the self-torment that follows rash words. The restored sleep symbolises complete inner reconciliation — not just civility toward the returning son but genuine peace with what happened.

sk: स्वर्गे लोके न भयं किंचनास्ति न तत्र त्वं न जरया बिभेति | उभे तीर्त्वाशनायापिपासे शोकातिगो मोदते स्वर्गलोके ||
ro: svarge · loke · na · bhayaṁ · kiñcanāsti · na · tatra · tvaṁ · na · jarayā · bibheti | ubhe · tīrtvā · aśanāyā · pipāse · śokātigo · modate · svarga·loke ||
hi: नचिकेता बोला: 'स्वर्गलोक में किसी भी प्रकार का भय नहीं है। वहाँ न आप (मृत्यु) हैं, न वृद्धावस्था का डर। भूख और प्यास दोनों से परे, शोक से अतीत होकर, स्वर्गलोक में आनन्दित होता है।'
en: 'In the heavenly world there is no fear whatsoever. You (Death) are not there; no one fears old age. Having crossed beyond both hunger and thirst, beyond sorrow, one rejoices in the heavenly world.'

ws.h: किसी प्रकार का भी भय नहीं
ws.e: no fear whatsoever — emphatic negation: kiñcana (of any kind at all)
'You are not there' — Nachiketa addresses Death directly: in heaven, Death is absent
fears old age — jarā (old age) + bibheti (fears, 3rd sg. of √bhī)
hunger and thirst — the two primal bodily drives, absent in heaven
beyond sorrow — śoka (grief) + atiga (one who has gone beyond)

gr: na tatra tvam — 'You are not there': Nachiketa tells Death to its face that heaven is defined by Death's absence. The boldness is remarkable for a child. ubhe tīrtvā aśanāyā pipāse — 'having crossed beyond both hunger and thirst': the dual 'ubhe' refers to the pair; tīrtvā (absolutive of √tṝ, 'to cross') uses the river-crossing metaphor. modate svarga-loke — 'rejoices in the heavenly world': modate (enjoys, delights) is middle voice — the enjoyment is self-directed, inward.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.1.12 — The second boon begins. Nachiketa describes heaven as the absence of death, old age, hunger, thirst, and sorrow — and asks for the fire-knowledge that leads there. This boon is 'higher' than the first (cosmic rather than personal) but still within the realm of desire.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि स्वर्ग — जहाँ मृत्यु नहीं, जरा नहीं, शोक नहीं — फिर भी अनित्य है। स्वर्ग-सुख समाप्त होता है और जीव पुनः लौटता है। नचिकेता का दूसरा वरदान इसी अनित्य सुख के लिए है — सच्चा ज्ञान तीसरे वरदान में आयेगा।
advaita.en: Shankara says heaven — where there is no death, no old age, no sorrow — is still impermanent. Heavenly joy ends and the soul returns. Nachiketa's second boon is for this impermanent joy — true knowledge will come with the third boon.
advaita.ins: Heaven is the highest reward of desire, but it is still within the realm of the finite. Liberation (mokṣa) is beyond even heaven.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि स्वर्ग भगवान् के निकट होने का एक स्तर है — शोक, भय और मृत्यु से परे। किन्तु परमपद (वैकुण्ठ) स्वर्ग से भी ऊँचा है — वहाँ पुनरावृत्ति नहीं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says heaven is one level of proximity to the Lord — beyond sorrow, fear, and death. But Paramapada (Vaikuṇṭha) is higher than heaven — there is no return from there.
vishisht.ins: Heaven is a station, not the destination. The soul's true home is the Lord's eternal abode.

aurobindo.h: अरविन्द स्वर्ग को चेतना की एक उच्चतर अवस्था मानते हैं — जहाँ भौतिक सीमाएँ (भूख, प्यास, जरा, मृत्यु) अनुपस्थित हैं। किन्तु यह अभी भी मानसिक स्वर्ग है — अतिमानसिक सत्य नहीं। नचिकेता का तीसरा वरदान उससे आगे जायेगा।
aurobindo.en: Aurobindo reads heaven as a higher state of consciousness where physical limitations (hunger, thirst, old age, death) are absent. But this is still a mental heaven — not the supramental truth. Nachiketa's third boon will go beyond.
aurobindo.ins: The heavenly consciousness is luminous but still bounded. The supramental truth includes and transforms the heavenly rather than merely escaping the earthly.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does Nachiketa tell Death 'You are not there' (na tatra tvam)?
dp.a: This is one of the boldest statements in the Upanishads: a child tells Death to its face that heaven is defined by Death's absence. The phrase na tatra tvam functions at multiple levels: (1) literal — in heaven, mortality does not exist; (2) rhetorical — by defining heaven as Death's absence, Nachiketa implicitly asks: 'If you know the way to a realm where you yourself cannot go, teach me that way'; (3) foreshadowing — the third boon will ask about something even beyond heaven: the Self that transcends both death and the absence of death.

dp.q: 🔍 How does the second boon differ from the first and third?
dp.a: The three boons map a hierarchy: First (personal/social) — restore my father's love; Second (cosmic/ritual) — teach me the fire that leads to heaven; Third (ultimate/metaphysical) — what happens after death? The second boon occupies the middle position — it is about cosmic knowledge (the Nachiketa fire ritual) but still within the framework of desire (wanting heaven). It is 'higher' than family reconciliation but 'lower' than Self-knowledge. This structural progression mirrors the Vedic hierarchy: kāmya-karma (desire-driven ritual) → upāsanā (meditation/worship) → jñāna (knowledge). Nachiketa climbs the ladder from the bottom, showing the Upanishad's acknowledgment that most seekers begin with desire and only gradually arrive at the desireless question.

sk: स त्वमग्निं स्वर्ग्यमध्येषि मृत्यो प्रब्रूहि त्वं श्रद्दधानाय मह्यम् | स्वर्गलोका अमृतत्वं भजन्त एतद्द्वितीयेन वृणे वरेण ||
ro: sa · tvam · agniṁ · svargyam · adhyeṣi · mṛtyo · prabrūhi · tvaṁ · śraddadhānāya · mahyam | svarga·lokā · amṛtatvaṁ · bhajanta · etad · dvitīyena · vṛṇe · vareṇa ||
hi: 'आप उस अग्नि को जानते हैं जो स्वर्ग की ओर ले जाती है, हे मृत्यो! श्रद्धावान् मुझे उसे बताइए। स्वर्गवासी अमृतत्व को प्राप्त होते हैं — यही मैं दूसरे वरदान में माँगता हूँ।'
en: 'You know the fire that leads to heaven, O Death. Teach it to me who am full of faith. The inhabitants of heaven enjoy immortality. This I choose as my second boon.'

ws.e: you know — 2nd sg. present of adhi+√i ('to study, know thoroughly')
to the faithful one — dative present participle of śrad+√dhā ('to place faith'); 'to me who has faith'
immortality — amṛta (deathless) + -tva (state of); the condition of being beyond death
they partake of, enjoy — present middle of √bhaj ('to share, enjoy')
as the second boon — instrumental: 'by means of the second boon'

gr: sa tvam agniṁ svargyam adhyeṣi — 'You yourself know the heavenly fire': the emphasis on 'tvam' (you) acknowledges Yama's unique authority — as the son of the Sun and lord of the departed, he knows the path to heaven. śraddadhānāya mahyam — 'to me who has faith': Nachiketa's self-description echoes mantra 2 where śraddhā entered him. He presents himself as a qualified student. dvitīyena vṛṇe vareṇa — the formal language of boon-selection.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.1.13 — Nachiketa formally requests the second boon: knowledge of the Nachiketa fire. He appeals both to Yama's knowledge (you know this fire) and to his own qualification (I am faithful). The verse introduces the theme of amṛtatva (immortality) that will dominate the rest of the Upanishad.

advaita.h: शंकर बताते हैं कि 'अमृतत्वम्' यहाँ सापेक्ष अमरत्व है — स्वर्ग की दीर्घ आयु, जो अन्ततः समाप्त होती है। तृतीय वरदान में पूछा जाने वाला 'अमृतत्व' पूर्ण और शाश्वत होगा।
advaita.en: Shankara clarifies that 'amṛtatva' here is relative immortality — the long life of heaven, which eventually ends. The 'immortality' asked about in the third boon will be absolute and eternal.
advaita.ins: There are degrees of immortality. Heaven's deathlessness is long duration; the Self's deathlessness is beyond time entirely.

vishisht.h: रामानुज श्रद्धा पर बल देते हैं — 'श्रद्दधानाय' — नचिकेता कहता है 'मुझमें श्रद्धा है।' भगवान् श्रद्धावान् को ही ज्ञान देते हैं; शुष्क बुद्धिवाद ज्ञान का पात्र नहीं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja emphasises faith — 'śraddadhānāya' — Nachiketa declares 'I have faith.' The Lord gives knowledge only to the faithful; dry intellectualism is not a vessel for knowledge.
vishisht.ins: Faith is not the absence of reason but the presence of trust. Only the trusting heart can receive the deepest teachings.

aurobindo.h: अरविन्द अग्नि को रूपान्तरण की शक्ति मानते हैं। 'स्वर्ग्य अग्नि' वह शक्ति है जो भौतिक चेतना को उच्चतर स्तर पर ले जाती है। नचिकेता इस रूपान्तरण-शक्ति का ज्ञान माँग रहा है।
aurobindo.en: Aurobindo reads the fire as the power of transformation. The 'heavenly fire' is the power that lifts physical consciousness to a higher level. Nachiketa is asking for knowledge of this transformative power.
aurobindo.ins: The Nachiketa fire is the aspiration that transforms the mortal into the immortal — not by destroying the mortal but by lifting it.

dp.q: 🔍 What is the 'heavenly fire' (agni svargya) that Nachiketa asks about?
dp.a: The Nachiketa fire (Nāciketāgni) is a specific fire-ritual (agni-vidyā) that Yama teaches. In the Vedic context, it involves building a fire-altar with specific bricks in specific numbers — a ritual technology for ascending to the heavenly world. But the Upanishad transforms this ritual into a symbol: the 'fire' is the inner aspiration that burns away mortality and lifts consciousness toward the immortal. The Taittiriya Brahmana describes a three-fold fire (tri-Nāciketa) that must be built three times — the repetition signifying thoroughness. Yama will teach both the outer ritual and its inner meaning.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does Nachiketa emphasise his faith (śraddadhānāya)?
dp.a: In the Vedic teaching tradition, the student must declare their qualification. Nachiketa's 'śraddadhānāya mahyam' (to me who has faith) is not boasting but a formal self-certification. The teacher has the right to withhold teaching from an unqualified student. By declaring his faith, Nachiketa removes Yama's excuse for refusal. This will become critical for the third boon: when Yama tries to refuse, Nachiketa can appeal to his demonstrated qualification — 'I am faithful and worthy; you cannot withhold the teaching.' The declaration of faith in the second boon becomes the leverage for extracting the third.

sk: प्र ते ब्रवीमि तदु मे निबोध स्वर्ग्यमग्निं नचिकेतः प्रजानन् | अनन्तलोकाप्तिमथो प्रतिष्ठां विद्धि त्वमेतं निहितं गुहायाम् ||
ro: pra · te · bravīmi · tad · u · me · nibodha · svargyam · agniṁ · naciketaḥ · prajānan | ananta·loka·āptim · atho · pratiṣṭhāṁ · viddhi · tvam · etaṁ · nihitaṁ · guhāyām ||
hi: यम बोले: 'मैं तुम्हें बताता हूँ, ध्यान से सुनो, हे नचिकेता! मैं स्वर्गीय अग्नि को भलीभाँति जानता हूँ। जान लो — यह अग्नि अनन्त लोकों की प्राप्ति और सबका आधार है — यह गुहा (हृदय) में छिपी है।'
en: Yama said: 'I will tell you — listen well, O Nachiketa. I know the heavenly fire. Know that this fire, which is the attainment of infinite worlds and their foundation, is hidden in the cave (of the heart).'

ws.e: listen, understand — imperative of ni+√budh ('to awaken to, comprehend')
knowing well — present participle of pra+√jñā; Yama affirms his own knowledge
the attainment of infinite worlds — ananta (infinite) + loka (world) + āpti (attainment)
foundation, support — the fire is the ground on which everything rests
hidden in the cave — nihita (placed, deposited) + guhā (cave, secret place; the heart)

gr: pra te bravīmi — 'I declare to you': pra- intensifies — this is a formal declaration, not casual speech. nihitaṁ guhāyām — 'hidden in the cave': guhā is the most significant word — it refers simultaneously to the heart-cave, the secret place of consciousness, and the ritual fire-pit. This phrase will recur throughout the Katha Upanishad as a leitmotif: the ultimate reality is always 'hidden in the cave.'
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.1.14 — Yama begins teaching the Nachiketa fire. The key phrase 'nihitaṁ guhāyām' (hidden in the cave) introduces the Katha Upanishad's central metaphor — the Self/Brahman hidden in the cave of the heart. What begins as a ritual instruction becomes a pointer to the innermost reality.

advaita.h: शंकर 'गुहायाम्' को बुद्धि की गुहा (intellect-cave) मानते हैं — आत्मा बुद्धि में, हृदय में, चेतना के गहनतम स्थान में छिपी है। अग्नि-विद्या बाह्य अनुष्ठान और आन्तरिक ध्यान दोनों है।
advaita.en: Shankara reads 'guhāyām' as the cave of the intellect — the Self is hidden in the buddhi, in the heart, in the deepest place of consciousness. The fire-knowledge is both outer ritual and inner meditation.
advaita.ins: The cave is not a physical location but the innermost recess of awareness. Brahman is 'hidden' only because we look outward.

vishisht.h: रामानुज 'गुहा' को हृदय-कमल मानते हैं — जहाँ भगवान् अन्तर्यामी रूप में विराजमान हैं। अग्नि-विद्या भगवान् तक पहुँचने का साधन है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja reads 'guhā' as the heart-lotus where the Lord resides as the inner controller (antaryāmi). The fire-knowledge is the means of reaching the Lord.
vishisht.ins: The Lord dwells in every heart. The fire of devotion reveals what is already present.

aurobindo.h: अरविन्द 'गुहा' को चेतना की गहनतम गुफा — अन्तरात्मा (psychic being) का निवास — मानते हैं। अग्नि वह अभीप्सा है जो इस गहराई से उठती है और चेतना को रूपान्तरित करती है।
aurobindo.en: Aurobindo reads 'guhā' as the deepest cave of consciousness — the dwelling of the psychic being. The fire is the aspiration that rises from this depth and transforms consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: The secret fire of aspiration burns in the heart's cave. It is always there — the practice is to find and tend it.

dp.q: 🔍 What does 'hidden in the cave' (nihitaṁ guhāyām) mean?
dp.a: This phrase — nihitaṁ guhāyām — is the Katha Upanishad's signature expression. It appears here for the first time and will recur throughout. Guhā means 'cave, secret place' — in the Upanishadic context, the 'cave of the heart' (hṛdaya-guhā). The fire/Self/Brahman is 'hidden' (nihita — placed, deposited) there — not because it is far away but because it is too close to see. We search outward for what is deposited in the innermost recess of our own being. The metaphor works on three levels: (1) the ritual fire-pit is a physical 'cave'; (2) the heart is the cave where the Self resides; (3) consciousness itself is the cave — the deepest layer of awareness where the Absolute rests, unnoticed by the surface mind.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does Yama call the fire both 'attainment of infinite worlds' and 'foundation'?
dp.a: The two terms — anantalokāpti (attainment of infinite worlds) and pratiṣṭhā (foundation) — point upward and downward simultaneously. The fire leads up to infinite worlds (the heavenly realms of cosmic experience) and is simultaneously the ground on which everything rests. This dual nature foreshadows the Katha's teaching about the Self: the Self is both the transcendent goal (what you seek to reach) and the immanent foundation (what you already stand on). The fire-knowledge is the first hint of this paradox — you are seeking what is already the ground of your being.

sk: लोकादिमग्निं तमुवाच तस्मै या इष्टका यावतीर्वा यथा वा | स चापि तत्प्रत्यवदद्यथोक्तं अथास्य मृत्युः पुनरेवाह तुष्टः ||
ro: lokādim · agniṁ · tam · uvāca · tasmai · yā · iṣṭakā · yāvatīr · vā · yathā · vā | sa · ca · api · tat · pratyavadad · yathoktaṁ · atha · asya · mṛtyuḥ · punar · eva · āha · tuṣṭaḥ ||
hi: यम ने उसे लोकों के आदि (मूल) अग्नि का ज्ञान दिया — कौन-सी ईंटें, कितनी, और कैसे रखी जाएँ। नचिकेता ने वह सब ठीक वैसे ही दोहरा दिया जैसा कहा गया था। तब मृत्यु ने प्रसन्न होकर पुनः कहा —
en: Yama taught him the fire — the origin of the worlds — what bricks, how many, and how arranged. Nachiketa repeated it exactly as told. Then Death, pleased, spoke again —

ws.e: origin of the worlds — loka (world) + ādi (beginning); the fire from which worlds arise
bricks — the specific bricks used to construct the fire-altar
repeated back — imperfect of prati+ava+√vad ('to say back, recite in response')
as stated — yathā (as) + ukta (spoken); exactly as taught, without error
pleased, satisfied — past participle of √tuṣ ('to be pleased')

gr: lokādim agnim — 'the fire that is the origin of worlds': this identifies the Nachiketa fire not merely as a ritual technique but as a cosmological principle — the creative fire from which existence emanates. yā iṣṭakā yāvatīr vā yathā vā — 'what bricks, how many, how arranged': the ritual details are compressed into a single phrase — the Upanishad is not interested in the technical specifications but in what they represent. pratyavadad yathoktam — 'repeated exactly as told': Nachiketa's perfect recall demonstrates his extraordinary qualification as a student.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.1.15 — The fire-teaching is summarised in a single verse — the Upanishad deliberately compresses the ritual detail to focus on its spiritual significance. Nachiketa's perfect recitation (pratyavadad yathoktam) demonstrates the ideal student's capacity: faithful, attentive, capable of exact reproduction.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि अग्नि-विद्या का विस्तार यहाँ जानबूझकर संक्षिप्त किया गया है — उपनिषद् का उद्देश्य अनुष्ठान-विधि नहीं, आत्मज्ञान है। नचिकेता का 'यथोक्तम्' कहना आदर्श शिष्य का लक्षण है — जो सुना, वैसा ही ग्रहण किया।
advaita.en: Shankara notes the fire-teaching is deliberately compressed here — the Upanishad's purpose is not ritual instruction but Self-knowledge. Nachiketa's 'yathoktam' (exactly as told) marks the ideal student — faithful reception without distortion.
advaita.ins: The best student receives the teaching as it is — without adding, subtracting, or reinterpreting. This fidelity is what pleases the teacher.

vishisht.h: रामानुज नचिकेता की बुद्धि-तीक्ष्णता और श्रद्धा की प्रशंसा करते हैं। गुरु-वचन को यथावत् ग्रहण करना भक्ति का एक रूप है — यह दर्शाता है कि शिष्य ने अपना अहंकार त्यागकर गुरु-वचन को प्राथमिकता दी।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja praises Nachiketa's intellectual sharpness and faith. Receiving the teacher's word exactly is a form of devotion — it shows the student has set aside ego to prioritise the teacher's word.
vishisht.ins: Perfect receptivity to the guru's teaching is itself an act of surrender.

aurobindo.h: अरविन्द कहते हैं कि नचिकेता का यथावत् दोहराना मन की उस शुद्धता का प्रमाण है जो उसे तीसरे वरदान के योग्य बनाएगी। जो मन गुरु-वचन को विकृत नहीं करता, वही आत्म-ज्ञान ग्रहण कर सकता है।
aurobindo.en: Aurobindo says Nachiketa's exact repetition proves the mental purity that will qualify him for the third boon. A mind that does not distort the teacher's word is the mind capable of receiving Self-knowledge.
aurobindo.ins: Clarity of reception precedes depth of understanding. The transparent mind receives the higher light undistorted.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does the Upanishad compress the entire fire-teaching into one verse?
dp.a: The Nachiketa fire-ritual, described in detail in the Taittiriya Brahmana, involves elaborate altar construction with specific bricks, numbers, and arrangements. The Katha Upanishad compresses all of this into a single phrase: 'what bricks, how many, how arranged' (yā iṣṭakā yāvatīr vā yathā vā). This compression is deliberate: the Upanishad is not a ritual manual but a wisdom text. The fire-ritual is acknowledged and honoured — but the Upanishad's focus is elsewhere. By compressing the second boon into minimal space, the text creates maximum room for the third boon (the question of death and immortality), which is the real teaching. The compression is itself a teaching: ritual knowledge, however valuable, is preparatory — not ultimate.

dp.q: 🔍 Why is Yama pleased (tuṣṭaḥ) by Nachiketa's recitation?
dp.a: Yama's pleasure goes beyond pedagogical satisfaction. A teacher who gives complex knowledge is naturally pleased when the student demonstrates perfect comprehension. But tuṣṭaḥ carries a deeper resonance: Yama is pleased because Nachiketa has proven himself a worthy recipient. This worthiness will become the ground on which Nachiketa stands when requesting the third boon. When Yama tries to deflect the third question, Nachiketa can silently point to this moment: 'You yourself declared me worthy. You were pleased with my reception. Now teach me the rest.' The teacher's pleasure becomes the student's leverage.

sk: तमब्रवीत्प्रीयमाणो महात्मा वरं तवेहाद्य ददामि भूयः | तवैव नाम्ना भवितायमग्निः सृङ्कां चेमामनेकरूपां गृहाण ||
ro: tam · abravīt · prīyamāṇo · mahātmā · varaṁ · tava · iha · adya · dadāmi · bhūyaḥ | tava · eva · nāmnā · bhavitā · ayam · agniḥ · sṛṅkāṁ · ca · imām · aneka·rūpāṁ · gṛhāṇa ||
hi: वह महात्मा (यम) प्रसन्न होकर बोला: 'आज मैं तुम्हें एक और वरदान देता हूँ। यह अग्नि तुम्हारे ही नाम से जानी जाएगी। और यह बहुरूपी सृंखला (अनेक रूपों वाली माला) भी ग्रहण करो।'
en: The great soul (Yama), being pleased, said to him: 'I give you yet another boon today. This fire shall bear your very name. Accept also this many-formed garland.'

ws.e: being pleased — present middle participle of √prī ('to delight'); Yama's delight continues from the previous verse
great soul — mahā (great) + ātman (self/soul); an epithet of genuine respect for Yama
additionally, moreover — an extra, unsolicited boon beyond the three
by name — instrumental: the fire will be called 'Nachiketa'
garland, chain — a many-formed ornamental chain; symbolising the interconnected chain of existence
many-formed — aneka (many) + rūpa (form); the diversity of manifestation

gr: prīyamāṇo mahātmā — 'the great soul, being pleased': Yama is called mahātmā — the Upanishad does not demonise Death but honours it as a great being. varaṁ tava iha adya dadāmi bhūyaḥ — 'I give you yet another boon today': this is beyond the three promised — a bonus born of genuine pleasure. tava eva nāmnā bhavitā ayam agniḥ — 'this fire shall bear your name': the Nachiketa fire becomes an institution. sṛṅkāṁ anekarūpām — the 'many-formed garland/chain' is variously interpreted: an ornament, a symbol of cosmic diversity, or the chain of karmic consequence.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.1.16 — Yama, delighted beyond obligation, adds a bonus: the fire will be named after Nachiketa, and he receives a symbolic garland. Death's generosity here contrasts with the difficulty of the third boon — Yama gives freely when the question is within his domain.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि यम का 'महात्मा' कहा जाना दर्शाता है कि मृत्यु एक दिव्य शक्ति है, शत्रु नहीं। अतिरिक्त वरदान और अग्नि का नामकरण नचिकेता की योग्यता की मुहर है।
advaita.en: Shankara notes that calling Yama 'mahātmā' shows Death is a divine power, not an enemy. The bonus boon and naming of the fire seal Nachiketa's qualification.
advaita.ins: Death is a teacher, not a destroyer. When approached with faith and courage, even Death gives more than asked.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि यम का प्रसन्न होकर अतिरिक्त देना भगवान् की कृपा का प्रतिबिम्ब है — भगवान् हमेशा अपेक्षा से अधिक देते हैं। अग्नि का नामकरण दर्शाता है कि सच्चे शिष्य का नाम शाश्वत हो जाता है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says Yama's pleased giving reflects the Lord's grace — the Lord always gives more than expected. Naming the fire shows that a true student's name becomes eternal.
vishisht.ins: The Lord's generosity exceeds all asking. A sincere offering receives an overflowing return.

aurobindo.h: अरविन्द 'अनेकरूपा सृंखला' को अस्तित्व की विविधता की श्रृंखला मानते हैं — ब्रह्म से भौतिक जगत् तक विस्तृत। नचिकेता को यह माला मिलती है — अर्थात् वह विश्व-प्रक्रिया को जानता है।
aurobindo.en: Aurobindo reads the 'many-formed garland' as the chain of existence's diversity — from Brahman to the physical world. Nachiketa receives this garland — meaning he comprehends the world-process.
aurobindo.ins: Understanding the diversity of manifestation is preparation for understanding the unity behind it.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does Yama give a bonus boon beyond the three promised?
dp.a: Yama's additional gift reveals a crucial aspect of the teacher-student relationship in the Upanishadic tradition. A truly pleased teacher does not merely fulfill an obligation — genuine delight in the student's capacity overflows into additional teaching. The three boons were a debt (for three nights' neglect). The bonus is pure grace — Yama gives because he is genuinely moved by Nachiketa's quality. This sets up a powerful contrast: for the second boon (fire-knowledge), Yama gives freely and abundantly. For the third boon (death's secret), he will resist desperately. The abundance here makes the reluctance there all the more dramatic.

dp.q: 🔍 What does it mean for the fire to 'bear Nachiketa's name'?
dp.a: The naming of the fire — Nāciketāgni — is an act of immortalisation within the ritual tradition. The boy who was 'given to Death' now has his name preserved for all time in one of the most important fire-rituals. The irony is exact: the father tried to sacrifice his son; instead, the son becomes the name of the sacrifice itself. Death, which should have ended Nachiketa's story, instead begins his eternal legacy. This is the Upanishad's first demonstration of its central teaching: the encounter with death, properly met, leads not to annihilation but to immortality.

sk: त्रिणाचिकेतस्त्रिभिरेत्य सन्धिं त्रिकर्मकृत्तरति जन्ममृत्यू | ब्रह्मजज्ञं देवमीड्यं विदित्वा निचाय्येमां शान्तिमत्यन्तमेति ||
ro: tri·ṇāciketaḥ · tribhir · etya · sandhiṁ · tri·karma·kṛt · tarati · janma·mṛtyū | brahma·jajñaṁ · devam · īḍyaṁ · viditvā · nicāyya · imāṁ · śāntim · atyantam · eti ||
hi: त्रिणाचिकेत (तीन बार अग्नि-चयन करने वाला), तीन सन्धियों (बन्धनों) को प्राप्त कर, तीन कर्म करके, जन्म और मृत्यु से तर जाता है। ब्रह्म से उत्पन्न, स्तुत्य देव को जानकर और उसका ध्यान करके, शाश्वत शान्ति को प्राप्त होता है।
en: The three-fold Nachiketa, having achieved the three connections and performing the three-fold work, crosses beyond birth and death. Knowing the adorable god born from Brahman, and realising this, one attains eternal peace.

ws.h: तीन बार नचिकेत-अग्नि चयन करने वाला
ws.e: the three-fold Nachiketa — one who has built the Nachiketa fire three times
connection, junction — the three connections: with mother, father, and teacher (or the three Vedas)
performer of three-fold work — sacrifice, study, and charity (or the three daily rituals)
crosses beyond birth and death — tarati (crosses, 3rd sg. of √tṝ)
born from Brahman — brahma + jajña (perfect participle of √jan, 'born')
peace utterly, eternal peace — atyanta (absolute, ultimate)

gr: tri-ṇāciketaḥ — the triple building of the Nachiketa fire: three-fold signifies completeness and mastery. tribhir etya sandhim — the 'three connections' are variously interpreted: the three relationships (mother, father, teacher), the three Vedas (Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma), or the three states (waking, dream, sleep). tarati janma-mṛtyū — 'crosses birth and death': the dual form (janma-mṛtyū) treats birth-and-death as a single compound reality to be transcended. śāntim atyantam eti — 'attains absolute peace': atyanta (beyond end) suggests a peace that has no terminus.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.1.17 — The verse describes the fruit of the three-fold Nachiketa fire: transcendence of the birth-death cycle and attainment of eternal peace. This is the highest promise of the ritual path — yet the third boon will ask about something even beyond this.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि यह श्लोक उपासना (meditation) का फल बताता है — जन्म-मृत्यु चक्र से मुक्ति। किन्तु यह क्रम-मुक्ति है (gradual liberation) — सीधी मुक्ति (immediate liberation) केवल आत्मज्ञान (तीसरे वरदान का विषय) से होती है।
advaita.en: Shankara says this verse describes the fruit of upāsanā (meditation) — freedom from the birth-death cycle. But this is gradual liberation (krama-mukti) — immediate liberation comes only through Self-knowledge (the subject of the third boon).
