advaita.ins: Ritual and meditation can free from the cycle gradually. Direct knowledge of the Self frees immediately.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि 'ब्रह्मजज्ञम् देवम्' भगवान् विष्णु हैं — ब्रह्म से प्रकट, सबके पूज्य। त्रिणाचिकेत अग्नि-विद्या भगवान् की उपासना का साधन है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja identifies 'brahmajajñam devam' as Lord Vishnu — manifest from Brahman, worthy of all worship. The three-fold fire-knowledge is a means of worshipping the Lord.
vishisht.ins: All ritual, properly understood, is worship of the Lord. The fire is the medium; the Lord is the destination.

aurobindo.h: अरविन्द तीन सन्धियों को तीन चेतना-स्तरों — भौतिक, प्राणिक और मानसिक — से जोड़ते हैं। तीनों को जोड़कर जो अग्नि प्रज्वलित होती है, वह जन्म-मृत्यु के चक्र को पार कराती है।
aurobindo.en: Aurobindo connects the three connections to three levels of consciousness — physical, vital, and mental. The fire that unites all three carries one beyond the birth-death cycle.
aurobindo.ins: True transformation integrates all levels of being. Partial awakening is not enough — the fire must burn at every level.

dp.q: 🔍 What are the 'three connections' (tribhir etya sandhim)?
dp.a: The three connections are interpreted differently by different authorities: (1) Three relationships: mother (mātṛ), father (pitṛ), and teacher (ācārya) — the three human sources of life, lineage, and knowledge. (2) Three Vedas: Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma — the three branches of sacred knowledge. (3) Three states: waking, dream, and deep sleep — the three modes of ordinary consciousness. All three readings converge: the seeker who has integrated all three relationships, all three knowledges, and all three states of consciousness achieves the complete fire — and this completeness is what carries one beyond birth and death.

dp.q: 🔍 How does this verse transition from the second to the third boon?
dp.a: This verse represents the highest promise of the ritual path: the three-fold Nachiketa fire, properly performed, leads to crossing beyond birth-death and attaining eternal peace. It is the culmination of the second boon. But notice what comes next (mantra 19): Yama says 'Choose your third boon.' The structure implies that even this magnificent promise — crossing beyond birth and death — is not the final word. Nachiketa will ask something that goes beyond even this: not 'how to reach heaven' or 'how to cross the cycle' but 'does the self exist after death?' The third boon transcends the second as knowledge transcends ritual — and this transition is the Katha Upanishad's central movement.

sk: त्रिणाचिकेतस्त्रयमेतद्विदित्वा य एवं विद्वांश्चिनुते नाचिकेतम् | स मृत्युपाशान्पुरतः प्रणोद्य शोकातिगो मोदते स्वर्गलोके ||

hi: त्रिणाचिकेत जो इन तीनों को जानकर, इस प्रकार विद्वान् होकर नाचिकेत अग्नि का चयन करता है — वह मृत्यु के पाशों को अपने सामने से दूर फेंककर, शोक से परे, स्वर्गलोक में आनन्दित होता है।
en: The three-fold Nachiketa, knowing these three, who thus knowing builds the Nachiketa fire — he, casting Death's nooses before him, beyond sorrow, rejoices in the heavenly world.

ws.e: these three — referring to the three-fold knowledge of the fire

ws.h: चयन करता है, चिता सजाता है
ws.e: builds, arranges — present middle of √ci ('to arrange, build the fire-altar')
Death's nooses — mṛtyu (death) + pāśa (noose, snare); the bonds of mortality
pushing away before oneself — purataḥ (in front) + praṇodya (absolutive of pra+√nud, 'to push away')
beyond sorrow — śoka (grief) + atiga (one who has gone beyond)

gr: ya evaṁ vidvāṁś cinute nāciketam — 'who, thus knowing, builds the Nachiketa fire': the emphasis on 'evaṁ vidvān' (knowing thus) shows that mere physical construction without understanding is insufficient. mṛtyu-pāśān purataḥ praṇodya — 'pushing Death's nooses away before him': the image is of a warrior casting off snares — active, forceful liberation. modate svarga-loke — 'rejoices in the heavenly world': same phrase as mantra 12, creating a frame — the second boon begins and ends with heavenly rejoicing.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.1.18 — The closing verse of the fire-teaching section. The image of 'casting Death's nooses' is powerful — the knower does not flee death but actively pushes its bonds aside. This verse concludes the second boon's teaching.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि 'मृत्युपाश' अविद्या, कामना और कर्म हैं — इन तीन बन्धनों को ज्ञानपूर्वक अग्नि-विद्या दूर करती है। किन्तु स्वर्ग अभी भी सशर्त मुक्ति है — शाश्वत मुक्ति आगे है।
advaita.en: Shankara identifies 'Death's nooses' as avidyā, desire, and karma — three bonds that the fire-knowledge dispels. But heaven is still conditional liberation — eternal liberation lies ahead.
advaita.ins: Breaking Death's bonds through knowledge of the fire is real — but it leads to heaven, not to the Absolute. The Absolute requires the third boon's teaching.

vishisht.h: रामानुज 'मृत्युपाश' को कर्म-बन्धन मानते हैं जो भगवद्-ज्ञान और उपासना से कटता है। स्वर्ग-प्राप्ति भक्ति-मार्ग का एक सोपान है — अन्तिम लक्ष्य परमपद है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja reads 'Death's nooses' as karmic bonds cut by the Lord's knowledge and worship. Reaching heaven is one step on the path of devotion — the ultimate goal is Paramapada.
vishisht.ins: Each level of liberation opens the door to a deeper one. Heaven is the doorway, not the dwelling.

aurobindo.h: अरविन्द कहते हैं कि 'पाशान् प्रणोद्य' (बन्धन दूर फेंकना) चेतना की सक्रिय मुक्ति है — निष्क्रिय स्वीकृति नहीं। साधक मृत्यु से नहीं भागता, बल्कि उसके बन्धनों को सक्रिय रूप से काटता है।
aurobindo.en: Aurobindo says 'pāśān praṇodya' (pushing away the bonds) is active liberation of consciousness — not passive acceptance. The seeker does not flee death but actively cuts its bonds.
aurobindo.ins: Liberation is not escape but conquest. The spiritual warrior actively pushes away the bonds of mortality.

dp.q: 🔍 What are 'Death's nooses' (mṛtyu-pāśa)?
dp.a: The image of Death's nooses (mṛtyu-pāśa) comes from Vedic mythology where Yama is depicted with a noose (pāśa) that he throws to capture the dying. In the Upanishadic context, these nooses are: avidyā (ignorance of one's true nature), kāma (desire that binds to rebirth), and karma (accumulated actions that compel future birth). The three-fold fire cuts these three nooses — each fold of the fire addresses one bond. The image of 'pushing them away before oneself' (purataḥ praṇodya) suggests the bonds don't disappear — they are still visible, but they no longer bind. The knower can see death's mechanisms without being caught by them.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does the verse say 'rejoices in heaven' rather than 'attains liberation'?
dp.a: The careful reader notices that the second boon's culmination is svarga-loka (heavenly world), not mokṣa (liberation). This is deliberate. The Nachiketa fire is a ritual achievement — it earns the highest possible reward within the ritual framework: heaven. But heaven, as Shankara repeatedly notes, is not the Absolute — it is the highest conditional state, still within saṁsāra. The third boon will ask about what lies beyond even heaven: the Self that neither comes nor goes. By ending the second boon at 'heaven,' the Upanishad creates the space for the third boon to transcend it completely.

sk: एष तेऽग्निर्नचिकेतः स्वर्ग्यो यमवृणीथा द्वितीयेन वरेण | एतमग्निं तवैव प्रवक्ष्यन्ति जनासः | तृतीयं वरं नचिकेतो वृणीष्व ||

hi: यम बोले: 'हे नचिकेता! यह तेरी स्वर्गीय अग्नि है जिसे तूने दूसरे वरदान में माँगा। लोग इस अग्नि को तेरे ही नाम से पुकारेंगे। अब तीसरा वरदान माँग, हे नचिकेता!'
en: 'This is your fire, O Nachiketa, the heavenly one, which you chose as your second boon. People will call this fire by your name alone. Choose now your third boon, O Nachiketa.'

ws.e: this is your fire — the fire is now formally Nachiketa's; the teaching is complete
you chose — imperfect middle 2nd sg. of √vṛ ('to choose'); past tense: the choosing is done
will proclaim — future 3rd pl. of pra+√vac ('to speak forth, declare')
people — nominative plural of jana; all people, for all time
choose the third boon — the invitation that opens the Upanishad's deepest teaching

gr: eṣa te agniḥ — 'this is your fire': the demonstrative 'eṣa' (this, right here) makes the gift tangible and present. tava eva pravakṣyanti janāsaḥ — 'people will call it by your name alone': eva (alone, only) emphasises the exclusivity — this fire belongs to Nachiketa forever. tṛtīyaṁ varaṁ vṛṇīṣva — the pivot of the entire Upanishad: 'Choose your third boon.' Everything before this was preparation; everything after is the teaching.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.1.19 — The hinge verse: Yama closes the second boon and opens the third. The instruction 'Choose your third boon' is the gateway to the Katha Upanishad's deepest teaching — the question of the Self's existence after death.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि यम ने दूसरा वरदान सहजता से दिया — क्योंकि अग्नि-विद्या उसके अधिकार-क्षेत्र में है। तीसरे वरदान पर यम की प्रतिक्रिया बिलकुल भिन्न होगी — क्योंकि वह प्रश्न यम के अपने अस्तित्व को चुनौती देता है।
advaita.en: Shankara says Yama gave the second boon easily — fire-knowledge is within his domain. His reaction to the third boon will be entirely different — because that question challenges Death's own existence.
advaita.ins: Death can teach about fire and heaven readily. But the question 'Does the Self survive death?' asks Death whether Death itself is ultimately real.

vishisht.h: रामानुज इस संक्रमण में भगवान् की योजना देखते हैं — दो वरदानों ने नचिकेता को तीसरे के लिए तैयार किया। पहले ने मानवीय बन्धन सुलझाया; दूसरे ने कर्मकाण्ड पूर्ण किया; तीसरा ज्ञान का शिखर होगा।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja sees the Lord's plan in this transition — two boons prepared Nachiketa for the third. The first resolved human bonds; the second completed ritual knowledge; the third will be the summit of wisdom.
vishisht.ins: Grace prepares the soul in stages: first settling the outer life, then completing ritual duty, then opening the door to ultimate knowledge.

aurobindo.h: अरविन्द 'तृतीयं वरं वृणीष्व' को चेतना के विकास में निर्णायक क्षण मानते हैं। पहला वरदान भौतिक-सामाजिक था; दूसरा प्राणिक-अनुष्ठानिक; तीसरा मानसिक-आध्यात्मिक — प्रत्येक चेतना के उच्चतर स्तर का द्वार खोलता है।
aurobindo.en: Aurobindo reads 'choose the third boon' as the decisive moment in the evolution of consciousness. The first boon was physical-social; the second vital-ritual; the third will be mental-spiritual — each opens the door to a higher level of consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: The soul's journey through the three boons mirrors consciousness's ascent through the three worlds: earth, mid-space, and heaven — and then beyond.

dp.q: 🔍 Why is 'Choose your third boon' the pivot of the entire Upanishad?
dp.a: Everything in the Katha Upanishad converges on this moment. The first two boons were preparation: the first (father's reconciliation) settled the human base; the second (fire-knowledge) completed the ritual superstructure. Now comes the question that the entire narrative exists to ask. When Yama says 'tṛtīyaṁ varaṁ vṛṇīṣva', he opens a door that he himself will try to close — because the third question (does the Self survive death?) is the one question Death cannot easily answer. Everything before this verse is setup; everything after is the teaching itself. The three-boon structure is a carefully engineered funnel: broad at the top (family concerns), narrower in the middle (cosmic ritual), and focused to a point at the bottom (the ultimate question of existence).

sk: येयं प्रेते विचिकित्सा मनुष्ये अस्तीत्येके नायमस्तीति चैके | एतद्विद्यामनुशिष्टस्त्वयाहमेतद्वराणां तृतीयं वरं वृणे ||

hi: 'मनुष्य के मरने पर जो यह संशय है — कुछ कहते हैं कि वह (आत्मा) है, कुछ कहते हैं कि नहीं है — इसे मैं आपसे सीखकर जानना चाहता हूँ। वरदानों में यह तीसरा वरदान मैं माँगता हूँ।'
en: 'There is this doubt about what happens when a man dies — some say he exists, others say he does not. I would know this, taught by you. Of the boons, this is the third boon I choose.'

ws.e: when departed, when dead — locative absolute of preta ('one who has gone forth, the departed')
doubt, questioning — from vi+√kit ('to question repeatedly'); intensive form implying deep, persistent doubt
'He exists,' say some — eke (some people); the affirmative position

ws.s: न अयम् अस्ति इति (na ayam asti iti)
ws.e: 'He does not exist,' say others — the negative position
instructed, taught — past participle of anu+√śās ('to teach, instruct'); 'being your student'

gr: yeyaṁ prete vicikitsā manuṣye — 'this doubt that exists when a man has died': the question is framed not about death in general but about a specific human being who has departed — 'this man, who was here, who has died — does he still exist?' asti iti eke na ayam asti iti ca eke — the two positions are stated with perfect symmetry: 'He is, say some; he is not, say others.' Neither position is favoured — the Upanishad presents genuine open inquiry. etad vidyām anuśiṣṭaḥ tvayā — 'I would know this, taught by you': Nachiketa positions himself as Yama's student, requesting formal instruction.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.1.20 — The most important verse of the Katha Upanishad: Nachiketa's third question. 'When a man dies — does he exist or not?' This is the fundamental question of all philosophy, all religion, all human inquiry into meaning. The rest of the Upanishad is Yama's answer.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि नचिकेता का प्रश्न मृत्यु के बाद जीवात्मा के अस्तित्व के बारे में नहीं — वह तो स्वतः-सिद्ध है। प्रश्न यह है: मृत्यु के बाद जो 'शेष' रहता है, वह क्या है? क्या वह सशरीर है, निराकार है, चैतन्य है, शून्य है? यही 'विचिकित्सा' (गहन संदेह) है।
advaita.en: Shankara says Nachiketa's question is not about whether a soul survives death — that is self-evident. The question is: what is it that 'remains'? Is it embodied, formless, conscious, void? This is the 'vicikitsā' (deep doubt).
advaita.ins: The question is not 'Is there life after death?' but 'What is the nature of that which does not die?' — a far subtler inquiry.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि प्रश्न आत्मा के स्वतन्त्र अस्तित्व के बारे में है — क्या जीव शरीर से अलग है? क्या वह भगवान् से भिन्न है? और मृत्यु के बाद उसकी गति क्या है? ये प्रश्न भक्ति-मार्ग के मूलाधार हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the question is about the soul's independent existence — is the jīva separate from the body? Is it different from the Lord? What is its destination after death? These questions are foundational to the path of devotion.
vishisht.ins: Without knowing the soul's nature, devotion has no ground. The third boon asks for that ground.

aurobindo.h: अरविन्द कहते हैं कि नचिकेता का प्रश्न मानव चेतना का केन्द्रीय प्रश्न है — क्या चेतना शरीर की उपज है (और मृत्यु में नष्ट होती है) या शरीर से स्वतन्त्र (और मृत्यु में बची रहती है)? यह प्रश्न भौतिकवाद और आध्यात्मिकता के बीच की विभाजन-रेखा है।
aurobindo.en: Aurobindo says Nachiketa's question is the central question of human consciousness: is consciousness a product of the body (and destroyed in death) or independent of it (and surviving death)? This question is the dividing line between materialism and spirituality.
aurobindo.ins: The answer to this question determines everything — ethics, meaning, purpose, and the entire direction of civilisation.

dp.q: 🔍 Why is this question so difficult that even Death hesitates to answer?
dp.a: The question 'When a man dies, does he exist or not?' is not a simple yes-or-no question — it is the most dangerous question in existence. If Death answers 'Yes, the Self survives death,' then Death has declared its own power limited — there is something Death cannot reach. If Death answers 'No,' it denies the foundation of all Vedic dharma. The question puts Death in an impossible position: to answer truthfully is to undermine its own authority. This is why Yama will try every possible deflection (temptation, distraction, intimidation) before finally answering. The question is not merely 'difficult to understand' — it is existentially threatening to the one being asked.

dp.q: 🔍 What does 'vicikitsā' (doubt) mean in this context?
dp.a: The word vicikitsā — from the intensive (frequentative) form of vi+√kit ('to question, to be aware') — means not casual doubt but persistent, deep, unresolved questioning. The intensive form implies: 'questioned again and again, examined repeatedly, still unresolved.' This is humanity's oldest and deepest uncertainty — does consciousness survive the body's destruction? Every civilisation, every philosophy, every individual who has lost someone faces this vicikitsā. The Upanishad's genius is to make this universal doubt the subject of a formal teaching — to bring it out of the realm of anxiety and into the realm of knowledge. Nachiketa does not merely wonder; he demands to know.

sk: देवैरत्रापि विचिकित्सितं पुरा न हि सुविज्ञेयमणुरेष धर्मः | अन्यं वरं नचिकेतो वृणीष्व मा मोपरोत्सीरति मा सृजैनम् ||

truth, law, nature — here meaning the fundamental nature of the Self after death

ws.h: इसे छोड़ दो, मुझे इससे मुक्त करो
ws.e: release me from this — ati (beyond) + mā (me) + sṛja (imperative of √sṛj, 'to release')

gr: devair atrā api vicikitsitam — 'even by the gods this was doubted': the argument from authority — if gods couldn't resolve this, how can a boy? aṇur eṣa dharmaḥ — 'this dharma is subtle': aṇu (atomic, infinitely small) — the truth is not gross enough to be grasped by ordinary means. mā mā uparotsīḥ — the doubled 'mā' (don't...me) shows genuine distress — Yama is not playing a game; he genuinely does not want to answer. ati mā sṛja enam — 'release me from this': Yama asks to be released — the lord of death asks a boy for freedom.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.1.21 — The beginning of Yama's resistance. Death tries to deflect the third question by invoking divine precedent (even gods doubted this), declaring its subtlety (aṇu), and directly asking to be released from the obligation. The temptation scene (mantras 22-25) follows.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि यम का प्रतिरोध अनुपयुक्त शिष्यों को छानने के लिए है। सच्चा गुरु कठिन ज्ञान तुरन्त नहीं देता — वह शिष्य की दृढ़ता परखता है। 'अणुः एष धर्मः' — यह सत्य इतना सूक्ष्म है कि केवल सर्वथा योग्य शिष्य ही ग्रहण कर सकता है।
advaita.en: Shankara says Yama's resistance is to filter out unworthy students. A true guru does not give difficult knowledge immediately — he tests the student's resolve. 'Aṇu eṣa dharmaḥ' — this truth is so subtle that only a completely qualified student can receive it.
advaita.ins: The guru's resistance is not refusal but testing. The teaching that costs nothing is worth nothing.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि यम की हिचकिचाहट दर्शाती है कि आत्म-ज्ञान भगवान् का सबसे गोपनीय रहस्य है — वह सहजता से नहीं दिया जाता। शिष्य की तीव्र जिज्ञासा ही इसे प्राप्त करने का एकमात्र उपाय है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says Yama's hesitation shows that Self-knowledge is the Lord's most guarded secret — it is not given lightly. Only the student's intense desire can obtain it.
vishisht.ins: The Lord's deepest teaching requires the deepest asking. Casual interest receives casual answers.

aurobindo.h: अरविन्द यम के प्रतिरोध को चेतना के विकास में एक प्राकृतिक बाधा मानते हैं — मृत्यु (सीमा, अन्त) का सिद्धान्त उस ज्ञान का विरोध करता है जो मृत्यु को अप्रासंगिक बना देगा। यम की असुविधा सत्य है — यह ज्ञान मृत्यु के अस्तित्व को ही खतरे में डालता है।
aurobindo.en: Aurobindo reads Yama's resistance as a natural barrier in the evolution of consciousness — the principle of Death (limit, ending) opposes the knowledge that would make death irrelevant. Yama's discomfort is real — this knowledge threatens Death's very existence.
aurobindo.ins: Every advance in consciousness faces resistance from the power it is about to transcend. Death resists the teaching of immortality because immortality makes death meaningless.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does Yama say 'Even the gods doubted this'?
dp.a: Yama's appeal to divine precedent — 'devair atrā api vicikitsitam purā' — is both a genuine statement and a deflection. It is genuine because the question of post-mortem existence is subtle beyond the reach of the sense-bound mind, even at the divine level. It is a deflection because Yama knows the answer and is trying to avoid giving it. The argument has the form: 'This is too difficult even for gods — surely you, a human boy, should not attempt it.' But Nachiketa will turn this argument against Yama: 'If even gods cannot know it, and you are the one teacher who can teach it, then this is precisely the boon I must ask of you and no other.'

dp.q: 🔍 What does it mean that Death asks a boy for release?
dp.a: The phrase 'ati mā sṛja enam' — 'release me from this' — is astonishing. Death asks to be released. The lord who binds all beings with his noose (mṛtyu-pāśa) is asking a boy to let him go. The power dynamic has completely reversed: in mantra 9, Yama offered boons from a position of obligation; now he is in a position of vulnerability. The question about the Self's survival after death is the one thing Death cannot comfortably address — because the answer (which Yama knows) is that the Self does survive, which means Death's power is not ultimate. To teach this truth is for Death to declare its own limitation. Yama's request for release is the cry of a power confronted by a truth greater than itself.

sk: देवैरत्रापि विचिकित्सितं किल त्वं च मृत्यो यन्न सुज्ञेयमात्थ | वक्ता चास्य त्वादृगन्यो न लभ्यो नान्यो वरस्तुल्य एतस्य कश्चित् ||
ro: devair · atrā · api · vicikitsitaṁ · kila · tvaṁ · ca · mṛtyo · yat · na · sujñeyam · āttha | vaktā · ca · asya · tvādṛk · anyo · na · labhyo · na · anyo · varas · tulya · etasya · kaścit ||
hi: नचिकेता बोला: 'आप स्वयं कहते हैं कि देवताओं को भी संशय हुआ और यह सहज-ज्ञेय नहीं है, हे मृत्यो! आपके समान कोई अन्य वक्ता इसका नहीं मिलेगा। इसके तुल्य कोई अन्य वर नहीं है।'
en: 'You yourself say that even the gods doubted this, and that it is not easily known, O Death. No other teacher of this subject like you can be found. No other boon equals this.'

ws.h: निश्चय ही, जैसा कि (आप ने कहा)
ws.e: indeed, as you say — particle referencing Yama's own words back to him
you say — 2nd sg. perfect of √ah ('to say')
speaker, teacher — agent noun of √vac; one who can teach this subject
like you — tvā + dṛk (appearance); 'of your kind, your equal'
equal — no boon matches this one in value

gr: devair atrā api vicikitsitaṁ kila — Nachiketa throws Yama's own argument back: 'You yourself said (kila) the gods doubted this.' tvādṛk anyo na labhyaḥ — 'no other like you is available': this is the decisive argument — if the question is so subtle that only the greatest teacher can answer it, and Yama is that teacher, then Nachiketa must ask Yama. The difficulty of the question becomes the reason to ask, not the reason to withdraw. na anyo varas tulyaḥ etasya — 'no other boon equals this': Nachiketa declares that this question is worth more than anything else Yama could offer.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.1.22 — Nachiketa's masterly counter-argument. He uses Yama's own deflection as leverage: if the question is so difficult that even gods couldn't answer it, then only you (Death) can teach it — and no substitute boon will do. The student's logic traps the teacher.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि नचिकेता का तर्क गुरु-परीक्षा उत्तीर्ण करता है। गुरु ने कहा 'कठिन है' — शिष्य ने कहा 'इसलिए मुझे आपसे ही सीखना है।' यह विवेक और वैराग्य का प्रमाण है — आत्मज्ञान के दो पूर्व-शर्त।
advaita.en: Shankara says Nachiketa's argument passes the guru's test. The guru said 'It is difficult' — the student replied 'That is exactly why I must learn from you.' This demonstrates viveka (discrimination) and vairāgya (dispassion) — the two prerequisites for Self-knowledge.
advaita.ins: The qualified student does not retreat before difficulty — he advances toward it. This advance is itself the proof of qualification.

vishisht.h: रामानुज नचिकेता की दृढ़ता को भक्ति की पराकाष्ठा मानते हैं — 'कोई अन्य वर इसके तुल्य नहीं' — यह दर्शाता है कि भगवद्-ज्ञान से बढ़कर कोई सम्पत्ति नहीं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja reads Nachiketa's firmness as the pinnacle of devotion — 'No other boon equals this' — showing that no wealth surpasses knowledge of the Lord.
vishisht.ins: The devotee who refuses all substitutes has passed the final test. God gives Himself only to one who will accept nothing less.

aurobindo.h: अरविन्द नचिकेता के तर्क में अन्तरात्मा की अडिग निश्चयशीलता देखते हैं। मन बहकाया जा सकता है, किन्तु आत्मा की खोज विचलित नहीं होती — यही 'श्रद्धा' की पूर्ण अभिव्यक्ति है।
aurobindo.en: Aurobindo sees in Nachiketa's argument the unshakeable determination of the psychic being. The mind can be distracted, but the soul's quest cannot be deflected — this is the full expression of śraddhā.
aurobindo.ins: When the soul has identified its question, nothing — not even Death's resistance — can divert it. This single-pointedness is the hallmark of the true seeker.

dp.q: 🔍 How does Nachiketa turn Yama's argument against him?
dp.a: This is one of the most intellectually brilliant moments in the Upanishads. Yama argued: this is too subtle — even gods doubted it — choose something else. Nachiketa responds: you just proved my case. His logic: (1) You say even gods couldn't resolve this — therefore no ordinary teacher can help. (2) You, Death itself, are the only qualified teacher — because you alone know what happens after death. (3) Therefore, I must ask you — there is no alternative. (4) And since there is no alternative, no substitute boon will do. Yama's deflection — meant to discourage — becomes Nachiketa's strongest argument for insisting. The subtlety of the question proves the indispensability of the teacher. The student uses the guru's own words as a bridge rather than a barrier.

sk: शतायुषः पुत्रपौत्रान्वृणीष्व बहून्पशून्हस्तिहिरण्यमश्वान् | भूमेर्महदायतनं वृणीष्व स्वयं च जीव शरदो यावदिच्छसि ||
ro: śatāyuṣaḥ · putra·pautrān · vṛṇīṣva · bahūn · paśūn · hasti·hiraṇyam · aśvān | bhūmer · mahad · āyatanaṁ · vṛṇīṣva · svayaṁ · ca · jīva · śarado · yāvad · icchasi ||
hi: यम बोले: 'सौ वर्ष जीने वाले पुत्र-पौत्र माँग ले, बहुत-से पशु, हाथी, सोना, घोड़े माँग ले। पृथ्वी पर विशाल राज्य माँग ले। और तू स्वयं जितने वर्ष चाहे जी ले।'
en: 'Choose sons and grandsons who live a hundred years; many cattle, elephants, gold, and horses. Choose a great domain of earth. And live yourself as many autumns as you wish.'

ws.e: living a hundred years — śata (hundred) + āyus (life); the maximum Vedic lifespan
sons and grandsons — the most coveted blessing: lineage and legacy
elephants and gold — symbols of royal wealth and power
domain, dwelling, estate — a great territory to rule
autumns (= years) — the Vedic way of counting years; 'as many years as you wish'

gr: śatāyuṣaḥ putrapautrān — the first temptation: long-lived descendants — lineage is the Vedic form of immortality. bahūn paśūn hasti-hiraṇyam aśvān — material wealth of every kind. bhūmer mahad āyatanam — 'a great domain of earth': political power, sovereignty. svayaṁ ca jīva śarado yāvad icchasi — 'and live yourself as long as you wish': the ultimate temporal boon — unlimited lifespan. Yama offers everything that can be desired within the mortal framework.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.1.23 — Yama's temptation begins in earnest. He offers the complete catalogue of worldly goods: descendants, wealth, power, and unlimited life. This is Death offering immortality's counterfeit — endless duration instead of timeless being.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि यम का प्रलोभन शिष्य की वैराग्य-परीक्षा है। जो साधक धन, यश, सन्तति और दीर्घायु को अस्वीकार कर सकता है — वही आत्मज्ञान का अधिकारी है। प्रलोभन जितना बड़ा, अस्वीकृति का मूल्य उतना अधिक।
advaita.en: Shankara says Yama's temptation is a test of the student's dispassion. Only the seeker who can refuse wealth, fame, progeny, and long life is qualified for Self-knowledge. The greater the temptation, the greater the value of refusal.
advaita.ins: The most powerful temptations are not sinful pleasures but the legitimate goods of life — family, wealth, power, longevity. Renouncing these for truth is the hardest test.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि यम का प्रस्ताव भगवान् के सिवाय सब कुछ है — और नचिकेता सब अस्वीकार करेगा क्योंकि भगवद्-ज्ञान के सामने सब तुच्छ है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says Yama's offer is everything except the Lord — and Nachiketa will refuse it all because everything is trivial compared to knowledge of the Lord.
vishisht.ins: The soul that has tasted even a glimpse of the Divine cannot be satisfied by the whole world.

aurobindo.h: अरविन्द इस प्रलोभन को प्रकृति (Nature) के प्रतिरोध के रूप में देखते हैं — चेतना जब ऊर्ध्वगामी होती है, तब प्रकृति अपने सर्वोत्तम आकर्षणों से उसे रोकने का प्रयास करती है।
aurobindo.en: Aurobindo reads the temptation as Nature's resistance — when consciousness moves upward, Nature tries to hold it back with her finest attractions.
aurobindo.ins: The greatest obstacle to the Transcendent is not evil but the good — the legitimate, beautiful, desirable goods that bind precisely because they are genuinely attractive.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does Yama tempt with 'legitimate goods' rather than sinful pleasures?
dp.a: The Upanishad's temptation scene is profoundly different from the typical 'temptation by evil.' Yama does not offer Nachiketa power over others, vengeance, or forbidden knowledge. He offers the best possible life: long-lived children, material prosperity, political power, and unlimited personal lifespan. These are not sins — they are the highest legitimate aspirations of the Vedic householder. The Upanishad's insight is that the deepest attachment is not to evil but to good. A seeker can easily renounce what is obviously harmful. The true test is renouncing what is genuinely good — family, wealth, a long and comfortable life — for something that cannot be seen or measured. Nachiketa's greatness is not that he rejects evil but that he rejects the best that the finite world can offer.

sk: एतत्तुल्यं यदि मन्यसे वरं वृणीष्व वित्तं चिरजीविकां च | महाभूमौ नचिकेतस्त्वमेधि कामानां त्वा कामभाजं करोमि ||
ro: etat · tulyaṁ · yadi · manyase · varaṁ · vṛṇīṣva · vittaṁ · cirajīvikāṁ · ca | mahā·bhūmau · naciketaḥ · tvam · edhi · kāmānāṁ · tvā · kāma·bhājaṁ · karomi ||
hi: 'यदि तू इसके बराबर कोई और वर समझे तो माँग ले — धन और दीर्घायु। हे नचिकेता, विशाल पृथ्वी पर राज कर! मैं तुझे सब कामनाओं का भोक्ता बना देता हूँ।'
en: 'If you think any boon equal to this, choose it — wealth and long life. Thrive on the great earth, O Nachiketa! I will make you the enjoyer of all desires.'

ws.e: equal, equivalent — Yama offers a substitute of 'equal' value
wealth — from √vid ('to find, obtain')
long life — cira (long) + jīvikā (living, livelihood)
thrive! — imperative 2nd sg. of √edh ('to prosper, grow')
enjoyer/sharer of desires — kāma (desire) + bhāj (one who shares/enjoys)

gr: etat tulyaṁ yadi manyase — 'if you consider any boon equal': Yama still tries to redirect — offering equivalence rather than direct refusal. kāmānāṁ tvā kāma-bhājaṁ karomi — 'I will make you the enjoyer of desires': the ultimate worldly offer — not just specific desires but the capacity to enjoy all desires. This is the structural maximum of what the finite world can offer.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.1.24 — Yama escalates the temptation: not just specific goods but the universal capacity to enjoy. 'I will make you the enjoyer of all desires' is the most comprehensive possible worldly offer — the blank cheque of mortality.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि 'कामभाजम्' — समस्त कामनाओं का भोक्ता — संसार का सर्वोच्च प्रस्ताव है। इससे अधिक लौकिक जगत् दे ही नहीं सकता। नचिकेता का अस्वीकार इसलिए सर्वोच्च वैराग्य है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'kāmabhājam' — enjoyer of all desires — is the world's highest offer. The temporal world cannot give more. Nachiketa's refusal is therefore the supreme dispassion.
advaita.ins: When you can refuse everything the world offers — not from inability to enjoy but from knowing something greater — that is true vairāgya.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि सभी कामनाओं का भोग भी भगवद्-ज्ञान के एक अंश के बराबर नहीं। भगवान् का प्रेम सब भोगों से परे है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says even enjoyment of all desires does not equal a fraction of knowledge of the Lord. The Lord's love surpasses all pleasures.
vishisht.ins: All the world's pleasures combined are a drop; the Lord's love is the ocean.

aurobindo.h: अरविन्द कहते हैं कि 'समस्त कामनाओं का भोक्ता' बनने का प्रस्ताव अहंकार का चरम विस्तार है — सब कुछ भोगना किन्तु सत्य को न जानना। यही माया का सर्वोच्च रूप है।
aurobindo.en: Aurobindo says the offer to become 'enjoyer of all desires' is the ego's ultimate expansion — to enjoy everything yet know nothing of the truth. This is the supreme form of māyā.
aurobindo.ins: The ego's dream of total enjoyment is the last and most seductive illusion. Beyond it lies the Self — which is beyond both enjoyment and its absence.

dp.q: 🔍 What is the difference between 'unlimited lifespan' and 'immortality'?
dp.a: Yama offers 'śarado yāvad icchasi' (as many years as you wish) and 'cirajīvikām' (long life). This is unlimited duration — living as long as you want within time. But this is not immortality (amṛtatva) in the Upanishadic sense. Immortality means existing beyond time altogether — not living for a very long time but being the eternal principle that is never born and never dies. Yama's offer is the counterfeit of what Nachiketa seeks: endless quantity of time versus timeless quality of being. This distinction is the Katha Upanishad's sharpest insight: even an infinite lifespan would not answer Nachiketa's question, because the question is not 'How long can I live?' but 'What am I beyond the body that lives and dies?'

sk: ये ये कामा दुर्लभा मर्त्यलोके सर्वान्कामांश्छन्दतः प्रार्थयस्व | इमा रामाः सरथाः सतूर्या न हीदृशा लम्भनीया मनुष्यैः | आभिर्मत्प्रत्ताभिः परिचारयस्व नचिकेतो मरणं मानुप्राक्षीः ||
ro: ye ye · kāmā · durlabhā · martya·loke · sarvān · kāmāṁś · chandataḥ · prārthayasva | imā · rāmāḥ · sa·rathāḥ · sa·tūryā · na · hīdṛśā · lambhanīyā · manuṣyaiḥ | ābhir · mat·prattābhiḥ · paricārayasva · naciketo · maraṇaṁ · mā · anuprākṣīḥ ||
hi: 'जो-जो कामनाएँ मृत्युलोक में दुर्लभ हैं, सब इच्छानुसार माँग ले। ये रमणियाँ — रथों और वाद्यों सहित — ऐसी मनुष्यों को प्राप्त नहीं होतीं। मेरे द्वारा दी हुई इनसे सेवा करा। हे नचिकेता, मरण के विषय में मत पूछ!'
en: 'Whatever desires are hard to obtain in the mortal world — ask for all desires at your pleasure. These fair maidens with their chariots and musical instruments — such are not to be won by mortals. Be served by these whom I give you. O Nachiketa, do not ask about death!'

ws.e: hard to obtain — dur (difficult) + labh (to get); the rarest pleasures
at pleasure, as you wish — from √chand ('to please'); complete freedom of choice
beautiful women — from √ram ('to delight'); celestial maidens
with chariots — sa (with) + ratha (chariot)
with musical instruments — sa (with) + tūrya (musical instrument)
do not ask — prohibitive aorist of anu+pra+√akṣ or √prach ('to ask'); 'stop inquiring about this'

gr: ye ye kāmā durlabhā martya-loke — 'whatever desires are hard to obtain in the mortal world': the doubling 'ye ye' (whatever, whatever) emphasises universality — anything at all. imā rāmāḥ sa-rathāḥ sa-tūryāḥ — the most vivid temptation: beautiful women with chariots and music — celestial pleasures ordinarily inaccessible to humans. na hīdṛśā lambhanīyā manuṣyaiḥ — 'such are not to be won by mortals': the exclusivity argument — what I offer is beyond mortal reach. maraṇaṁ mā anuprākṣīḥ — 'do not ask about death': Yama's final, desperate plea.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.1.25 — The climax of Yama's temptation: celestial maidens, unlimited pleasure, and a direct command not to ask about death. This is the temptation's most sensual moment — and Nachiketa's refusal (mantras 26-29) will be correspondingly magnificent.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि 'मरणं मा अनुप्राक्षीः' (मृत्यु के बारे में मत पूछ) यम का अन्तिम प्रयास है। शंकर इस पूरे प्रलोभन-दृश्य को शिष्य-परीक्षा मानते हैं — केवल वह शिष्य जो सब कुछ अस्वीकार करे, आत्मज्ञान का अधिकारी है।
advaita.en: Shankara reads 'maraṇaṁ mā anuprākṣīḥ' (don't ask about death) as Yama's final attempt. Shankara treats the entire temptation as a student-test — only the student who refuses everything is qualified for Self-knowledge.
advaita.ins: The ultimate examination is not intellectual but existential: can you refuse the world's best offer for an invisible truth?

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि स्वर्गीय रमणियाँ और भोग भगवान् के बिना शून्य हैं। नचिकेता यह जानता है — इसलिए वह अस्वीकार करेगा।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says celestial maidens and pleasures are empty without the Lord. Nachiketa knows this — therefore he will refuse.
vishisht.ins: No pleasure, however exalted, can substitute for the Lord's presence.

aurobindo.h: अरविन्द इस प्रलोभन को काम (desire) की अन्तिम चुनौती मानते हैं — चेतना के उत्थान के मार्ग में काम-शक्ति अपने सर्वोत्तम रूप में बाधा बनती है। इसे पार करना ही सच्ची विजय है।
aurobindo.en: Aurobindo reads this as desire's final challenge — on the path of consciousness's ascent, the desire-force presents its finest form as an obstacle. Crossing this is the true victory.
aurobindo.ins: The last barrier is not aversion but attraction. The soul must pass through desire's most beautiful manifestation to reach the Eternal.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does Yama end with 'Do not ask about death' (maraṇaṁ mā anuprākṣīḥ)?
dp.a: This is the most revealing moment of the temptation. After offering everything — descendants, wealth, power, pleasure, unlimited life, celestial maidens — Yama adds a direct prohibition: 'Do not ask about death.' The shift from enticement to command shows Yama's desperation. He has exhausted every positive inducement and now resorts to a bare directive. The word anuprākṣīḥ (from anu+pra+√prach, 'to inquire persistently') suggests that Nachiketa has been pressing this question throughout the temptation, undeterred. The boy's silence during the offers was not hesitation but the steady pressure of a question that refuses to be diverted. Yama's command reveals that the offers have failed — and the next verses will show Nachiketa's magnificent refusal.

sk: श्वोभावा मर्त्यस्य यदन्तकैतत्सर्वेन्द्रियाणां जरयन्ति तेजः | अपि सर्वं जीवितमल्पमेव तवैव वाहास्तव नृत्यगीते ||
ro: śvo·bhāvā · martyasya · yad · antaka · etat · sarva·indriyāṇāṁ · jarayanti · tejaḥ | api · sarvaṁ · jīvitam · alpam · eva · tava · eva · vāhāḥ · tava · nṛtya·gīte ||
hi: नचिकेता बोला: 'हे अन्तक (मृत्यो)! ये सब भोग कल तक ही रहने वाले हैं। ये सब इन्द्रियों का तेज क्षीण कर देते हैं। सम्पूर्ण जीवन भी अल्प ही है। आपके ही रहें आपके वाहन, आपके ही रहें नृत्य और गीत।'
en: 'These things last only till tomorrow, O Ender (Death). They wear out the vigour of all the senses. Even a whole life is but short. Keep your chariots, keep your dance and song.'

ws.e: lasting only till tomorrow — śvas (tomorrow) + bhāva (existence); ephemeral
O Ender — vocative of antaka; a name for Death meaning 'the one who ends'

ws.h: क्षीण करते हैं, जीर्ण करते हैं
ws.e: they wear out — causative of √jṝ ('to age, decay'); the pleasures themselves cause decay
vigour, radiance — the vital energy of the senses; depleted by indulgence
very little, mere trifle — eva intensifies: even a full life is just a trifle

gr: śvo-bhāvāḥ — 'things of tomorrow': a single compound that dismisses all temporal goods — they exist only until tomorrow, i.e., they are already passing even as you enjoy them. sarvendriyāṇāṁ jarayanti tejaḥ — the pleasures actively destroy the senses' capacity: indulgence leads to exhaustion. api sarvaṁ jīvitam alpam eva — 'even a whole life is but short': this is a boy — possibly no more than twelve years old — declaring that an entire human life is trivial. tava eva vāhāḥ tava nṛtya-gīte — 'Keep your chariots, keep your dance and song': the dismissal is contemptuous and absolute.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.1.26 — Nachiketa's magnificent refusal begins. In a single verse he dismisses all of Yama's offers with three arguments: (1) they are ephemeral (śvo-bhāvā); (2) they destroy the senses; (3) even a whole life is short. Then the devastating punchline: 'Keep your chariots; keep your dance and song.'

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि 'श्वोभावा' (कल तक रहने वाले) एक शब्द में सांसारिक सुखों का सम्पूर्ण खण्डन है। जो कल समाप्त हो जाये, उसके लिए शाश्वत सत्य को छोड़ना मूर्खता है। नचिकेता का वैराग्य यहाँ पूर्ण है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'śvo-bhāvā' (things of tomorrow) is a one-word refutation of all worldly pleasures. To abandon eternal truth for what ends tomorrow is folly. Nachiketa's dispassion is here complete.
advaita.ins: One word — 'tomorrow' — destroys the allure of every temporal pleasure. What lasts until tomorrow is already gone.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि नचिकेता की अस्वीकृति भगवद्-प्रेम की शक्ति से आती है — जो भगवान् को चाहता है, वह संसार को स्वतः अल्प जानता है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says Nachiketa's refusal comes from the power of love for the Lord — one who desires the Lord naturally knows the world as trivial.
vishisht.ins: The soul that has glimpsed the Eternal finds all temporal goods — however splendid — naturally trivial.

aurobindo.h: अरविन्द 'श्वोभावा' में अनित्यता (impermanence) का सर्वोच्च बोध देखते हैं। जब चेतना शाश्वत की ओर मुड़ती है, तब सब क्षणिक वस्तुएँ अपने आप गिर जाती हैं — त्याग करना नहीं पड़ता, वे अर्थहीन हो जाती हैं।
aurobindo.en: Aurobindo sees in 'śvo-bhāvā' the supreme insight into impermanence. When consciousness turns toward the Eternal, all transient things fall away naturally — one does not need to renounce them; they become meaningless.
aurobindo.ins: True renunciation is not painful rejection but natural irrelevance — the Eternal makes the temporal simply uninteresting.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does Nachiketa say pleasures 'wear out the senses' (jarayanti tejaḥ)?
dp.a: This is a remarkably sophisticated observation for a boy. Nachiketa does not say pleasures are evil — he says they are self-consuming. The word jarayanti (causative of √jṝ, 'to age') means the pleasures actively cause the senses to decay. The more you indulge, the less capacity you have to enjoy. This is not moral condemnation but psychological observation: pleasure has diminishing returns. The first taste delights; the hundredth taste barely registers. The senses that were meant to be instruments of perception become dulled by overuse. Nachiketa's argument is not ascetic ('pleasure is bad') but realistic ('pleasure destroys its own instrument').

dp.q: 🔍 What does 'Keep your chariots, keep your dance and song' reveal?
dp.a: The final line — 'tava eva vāhāḥ tava nṛtya-gīte' (yours be the chariots, yours the dance and song) — is Nachiketa's rhetorical masterstroke. He does not merely decline Yama's offer; he returns it. The phrasing 'tava eva' (yours only, yours alone) implies: 'These things belong to your world, O Death — the world of temporality, of endings, of things that last until tomorrow. I want no part of your world. I want what is beyond your world.' By returning the gifts to Death, Nachiketa symbolically declares that the entire domain of the finite — however beautiful — belongs to Death and is therefore inherently impermanent. He seeks the one thing that does not belong to Death: the deathless Self.

sk: न वित्तेन तर्पणीयो मनुष्यो लप्स्यामहे वित्तमद्राक्ष्म चेत्त्वा | जीविष्यामो यावदीशिष्यसि त्वं वरस्तु मे वरणीय एव सः ||
ro: na · vittena · tarpaṇīyo · manuṣyo · lapsyāmahe · vittam · adrākṣma · cet · tvā | jīviṣyāmo · yāvad · īśiṣyasi · tvaṁ · varas · tu · me · varaṇīya · eva · saḥ ||
hi: 'मनुष्य धन से सन्तुष्ट होने वाला नहीं। यदि हम आपको देख चुके हैं तो धन तो मिल ही जायेगा। हम तब तक जीएँगे जब तक आप (मृत्यु) शासन करें। परन्तु मेरा चुना हुआ वरदान वही (तीसरा) है।'
en: 'Man is not to be satisfied by wealth. We shall obtain wealth if we have seen you. We shall live only as long as you rule. The boon I choose is verily that alone.'

ws.e: cannot be satisfied — gerundive negative of √tṛp ('to be satisfied'); it is impossible to satisfy man with wealth
we shall obtain — future 1st pl. of √labh; wealth will come naturally
we have seen — aorist 1st pl. of √dṛś; 'having beheld you (Death)'
you will rule — future 2nd sg. of √īś ('to rule, command')
worthy of choosing — gerundive of √vṛ ('to choose'); 'the only one worth choosing'

gr: na vittena tarpaṇīyo manuṣyaḥ — 'man cannot be satisfied by wealth': a universal anthropological statement — the nature of desire is that it can never be fulfilled by its objects. lapsyāmahe vittam adrākṣma cet tvā — 'we shall get wealth having seen you': a sardonic aside — having met Death face-to-face, worldly wealth seems easy to obtain. jīviṣyāmo yāvad īśiṣyasi tvam — 'we shall live as long as you rule': since Death rules time, our lifespan is entirely in Death's hands — so offering long life is giving what is already Death's to give or take. varas tu me varaṇīya eva saḥ — the emphatic conclusion: 'that boon alone is worth choosing.'
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.1.27 — Nachiketa's refusal deepens: wealth cannot satisfy (a universal truth), lifespan is Death's to control (so offering it is circular), and the only boon worth choosing is the original question. The verse 'na vittena tarpaṇīyo manuṣyaḥ' is one of the most quoted lines in all Upanishadic literature.

advaita.h: शंकर 'न वित्तेन तर्पणीयो मनुष्यः' को मानव-स्वभाव का सार्वभौमिक सत्य मानते हैं। कामना की प्रकृति ही ऐसी है कि जितना मिले, उतनी और बढ़ती है। इसलिए कामना-पूर्ति से कभी तृप्ति नहीं होती — केवल ज्ञान से होती है।
advaita.en: Shankara reads 'na vittena tarpaṇīyo manuṣyaḥ' as a universal truth of human nature. Desire by its nature grows with fulfillment — more only produces more craving. Satisfaction comes only through knowledge, never through objects.
advaita.ins: The nature of desire is to increase with feeding. Only the knowledge of the desireless Self can end the cycle of craving.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि मनुष्य की अतृप्ति भगवान् के प्रति उसकी स्वाभाविक अभिलाषा का प्रमाण है — संसार की कोई भी वस्तु इस अभिलाषा को पूर्ण नहीं कर सकती, केवल भगवान् कर सकते हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says man's insatiability is proof of his natural longing for the Lord — no worldly object can fulfill this longing; only the Lord can.
vishisht.ins: Every unsatisfied desire is a misidentified desire for God.

aurobindo.h: अरविन्द कहते हैं कि मानव चेतना सीमित वस्तुओं से कभी सन्तुष्ट नहीं हो सकती क्योंकि चेतना स्वभावतः असीम है — वह असीम को ही खोज रही है, सीमित रूपों में।
aurobindo.en: Aurobindo says human consciousness can never be satisfied by finite objects because consciousness is inherently infinite — it is seeking the Infinite, disguised in finite forms.
aurobindo.ins: The soul's hunger is for the Infinite. Every finite satisfaction only sharpens that hunger.

dp.q: 🔍 Why is 'Man cannot be satisfied by wealth' (na vittena tarpaṇīyo manuṣyaḥ) so famous?
dp.a: This sentence is one of the most quoted in Indian philosophy because it captures a universal empirical truth in seven words. It is not a moral injunction ('you should not want wealth') but an observation about human nature ('wealth cannot satisfy you'). The gerundive tarpaṇīyaḥ (capable of being satisfied) makes it definitive — it is not that man should not be satisfied by wealth, but that he cannot be. The structure of desire is self-expanding: each fulfillment creates new desires. This is observable in every life, every society, every era. The Upanishad's insight predates and includes the Buddhist observation of dukkha, the Stoic concept of preferred indifferents, and the modern psychological understanding of hedonic adaptation — all captured in one verse, spoken by a boy to Death itself.

sk: अजीर्यतामृतानामुपेत्य जीर्यन्मर्त्यः क्वधःस्थः प्रजानन् | अभिध्यायन्वर्णरतिप्रमोदानतिदीर्घे जीविते को रमेत ||
ro: ajīryatām · amṛtānām · upetya · jīryan · martyaḥ · kva · adhaḥ·sthaḥ · prajānan | abhidhyāyan · varṇa·rati·pramodān · atidīrghe · jīvite · ko · rameta ||
hi: 'अजर-अमर (देवताओं) के निकट पहुँचकर, स्वयं जीर्ण होता हुआ, नीचे रहता हुआ मर्त्य प्राणी — रूप-रति-आमोद पर विचार करते हुए — अत्यन्त दीर्घ जीवन में भी कौन आनन्दित होगा?'
en: 'Having approached the undecaying immortals, what decaying mortal here below, knowing (his condition), reflecting on the pleasures of beauty and love — who would delight in an over-long life?'

ws.h: न जीर्ण होने वाले, अमर (देवताओं) के
ws.e: of the undecaying immortals — genitive pl.; those who neither age nor die
having approached — absolutive of upa+√i ('to go near')

ws.h: जीर्ण होता हुआ, बूढ़ा होता हुआ
ws.e: decaying — present participle of √jṝ ('to age'); even while approaching the immortals, the mortal is aging
dwelling below — adhaḥ (below) + stha (standing); mortals dwell in the lower realm
beauty, love-play, and delight — three categories of sensory pleasure
over-long — ati (excessively) + dīrgha (long); even unlimited lifespan

gr: ajīryatām amṛtānām upetya — 'having approached the undecaying immortals': Nachiketa has been in Yama's presence — he has already 'approached' the realm of the immortal. From this vantage point, mortal pleasures look trivial. jīryan martyaḥ kva adhaḥ-sthaḥ — 'what decaying mortal, dwelling below': the three conditions (decaying, mortal, below) stack to create a devastating portrait of the human condition. ko rameta — 'who would delight?': a rhetorical question expecting the answer 'no one.'
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.1.28 — Nachiketa's most philosophical argument: having glimpsed immortality, how can a decaying mortal find satisfaction in endless but declining life? The verse turns the temptation inside out — the very fact of having met Death reveals the emptiness of Death's offers.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि यह श्लोक विवेक का पूर्ण प्रकाश है: जो क्षणभंगुर है उसे शाश्वत के प्रकाश में देखना — यही ज्ञान का प्रारम्भ है। नचिकेता ने अमृत (यम) के समक्ष खड़े होकर अपनी नश्वरता को देखा — और उसी क्षण निर्णय हो गया।
advaita.en: Shankara says this verse is the full light of discrimination: seeing the transient in the light of the eternal — this is the beginning of knowledge. Standing before the immortal (Yama), Nachiketa saw his own mortality — and the decision was made.
advaita.ins: True discrimination arises when you see the finite from the standpoint of the Infinite. From there, no finite offer can tempt.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि 'अजीर्यताम् अमृतानाम् उपेत्य' — अमर देवताओं के पास जाकर — यह अनुभव भगवान् के दर्शन का पूर्व-स्वाद है। एक बार भगवान् की झलक पाने के बाद, संसार का कोई भी सुख आकृष्ट नहीं कर सकता।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'having approached the immortals' is a foretaste of the Lord's vision. Once you have glimpsed the Lord, no worldly pleasure can attract.
vishisht.ins: One moment of the Lord's darśana makes a lifetime of worldly pleasure seem like a shadow on the wall.

aurobindo.h: अरविन्द कहते हैं कि नचिकेता का दृष्टिकोण अब ऊर्ध्व से है — उसने अमरत्व का स्तर देखा है और नीचे लौटकर क्षणभंगुर सुखों में रमण करना असम्भव है। यह चेतना का अपरिवर्तनीय रूपान्तरण है।
aurobindo.en: Aurobindo says Nachiketa's perspective is now from above — he has seen the level of immortality and returning to revel in transient pleasures is impossible. This is an irreversible transformation of consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: Once consciousness has risen to a higher level, it cannot genuinely return to the lower. The view from the summit makes the valley's pleasures uninteresting.

dp.q: 🔍 What makes this argument Nachiketa's most devastating?
dp.a: Nachiketa's final argument before his concluding demand is a masterpiece of existential reasoning. He says: I have already approached the immortals (you, Yama, and your realm). From that vantage point, I can see what I am — a decaying mortal dwelling below. Knowing this, how could I possibly enjoy an over-long life? The argument works because it uses Yama's own gift against him. By sending Nachiketa to the realm of death, Yama inadvertently gave the boy the one experience that makes all worldly temptation powerless: the direct perception of mortality. Once you have truly seen that you are dying — not as an abstract idea but as a lived fact — no amount of beauty, love, or delight can make you forget. The encounter with Death, which Yama intended as an obligation, has become Nachiketa's liberation from desire.

sk: यस्मिन्निदं विचिकित्सन्ति मृत्यो यत्साम्पराये महति ब्रूहि नस्तत् | योऽयं वरो गूढमनुप्रविष्टो नान्यं तस्मान्नचिकेता वृणीते ||
ro: yasmin · idaṁ · vicikitsanti · mṛtyo · yat · sāmparāye · mahati · brūhi · nas · tat | yo · ayaṁ · varo · gūḍham · anupraviṣṭo · na · anyaṁ · tasmāt · naciketā · vṛṇīte ||
hi: 'हे मृत्यो! जिस महान् साम्पराय (परलोक) के विषय में यह संदेह है — वह हमें बताइए। जो यह वरदान गहनतम रहस्य में प्रविष्ट है — उसके सिवाय नचिकेता कुछ और नहीं माँगता।'
en: 'That about which they doubt, O Death — what lies in the great hereafter — tell us that. This boon that has entered into the deepest mystery — no other than this does Nachiketa choose.'

ws.e: they doubt — present 3rd pl. of intensive √kit; persistent, universal doubt
in the great hereafter — sāmparāya (the next world, the beyond) + mahati (great)
tell us — imperative of √brū + naḥ (to us); the plural 'us' includes all seekers

ws.h: गहन रहस्य में प्रवेश किया हुआ
ws.e: entered into the hidden/secret — gūḍha (hidden) + anupraviṣṭa (penetrated, gone deep into)
no other — emphatic refusal of all alternatives

gr: yasmin idaṁ vicikitsanti — 'that about which they doubt': the universal doubt, shared by gods and mortals alike. sāmparāye mahati — 'in the great hereafter': sāmparāya (from sam+parā+√i, 'that which lies beyond') + mahati (great) — the 'great beyond' is not a place but a question about the nature of existence itself. gūḍham anupraviṣṭaḥ — 'entered into the hidden': this boon has gone deep into mystery — it is not a surface question but one that penetrates to the core of reality. na anyaṁ tasmāt naciketā vṛṇīte — the closing statement: Nachiketa, speaking of himself in the third person for emphasis, declares with finality that he chooses nothing else.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_1.1.29 — The closing verse of Valli 1. Nachiketa's final, irrevocable demand: tell me what lies in the great hereafter. The speaking in third person ('Nachiketa chooses no other') gives the demand the force of an absolute declaration. Valli 2 will begin with Yama's response — the teaching of the Self.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि नचिकेता का 'गूढमनुप्रविष्ट' कहना दर्शाता है कि यह प्रश्न सतही नहीं — यह अस्तित्व के गहनतम रहस्य में प्रवेश करता है। 'ब्रूहि नः' में 'नः' (हमें) बहुवचन है — नचिकेता समस्त मानवता की ओर से पूछ रहा है। यहाँ शिष्य-परीक्षा पूर्ण हो चुकी है; अब गुरु को उत्तर देना ही होगा।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'gūḍham anupraviṣṭa' (entered into the hidden) shows this question is not superficial — it penetrates existence's deepest mystery. The plural 'naḥ' (us) means Nachiketa asks on behalf of all humanity. The student's testing is now complete; the teacher must answer.
advaita.ins: When the student has proven themselves absolutely — by refusing every substitute and insisting with total conviction — the teacher can no longer withhold. The teaching must flow.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि 'साम्पराये महति' — 'महान् परलोक' — भगवान् का नित्य धाम है। नचिकेता का प्रश्न वस्तुतः यह है: भगवान् तक कैसे पहुँचें और क्या वहाँ से लौटना होता है? यही भक्ति-मार्ग का सर्वोच्च प्रश्न है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'sāmparāye mahati' — 'the great beyond' — is the Lord's eternal realm. Nachiketa's question is really: how does one reach the Lord, and is there return? This is the supreme question of the devotion-path.
vishisht.ins: The ultimate question of every devotee: will I reach the Lord, and having reached, will I ever be separated again?

aurobindo.h: अरविन्द 'गूढमनुप्रविष्ट' में चेतना की गहनतम गुहा — अन्तरात्मा के रहस्य — की ओर संकेत देखते हैं। नचिकेता का प्रश्न सीधा मृत्यु के पार क्या है, यह नहीं — बल्कि 'चेतना का वह स्तर क्या है जो मृत्यु को पार करता है?'
aurobindo.en: Aurobindo sees in 'gūḍham anupraviṣṭa' a pointer to consciousness's deepest cave — the psychic being's mystery. Nachiketa's question is not simply 'what is beyond death' but 'what level of consciousness transcends death?'
aurobindo.ins: The question that enters the deepest mystery is not about a place after death but about the dimension of being that death cannot touch.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does Nachiketa speak of himself in the third person ('Nachiketa chooses no other')?
dp.a: The shift to third person — 'naciketā vṛṇīte' (Nachiketa chooses) instead of 'vṛṇe' (I choose) — is a rhetorical escalation. By naming himself, Nachiketa transforms his personal request into a historical declaration. He is no longer a boy asking a favour; he is a figure making a statement for the record. The third person gives the demand the quality of an oath, a public vow, an irrevocable commitment. It also creates distance between the speaker and the act — as if to say: 'This is not merely my whim; this is what Nachiketa — the one who bears this name, this destiny — is determined to do.' The declaration closes Valli 1 with absolute finality. There is no going back. Yama must now teach.

dp.q: 🔍 How does Valli 1 set up the rest of the Katha Upanishad?
dp.a: Valli 1 is a masterfully constructed prologue that establishes every element the Upanishad needs: (1) The seeker's qualification — Nachiketa has been tested by circumstances (his father's curse), by endurance (three nights without food), by intellectual capacity (perfect recall of the fire-teaching), and by dispassion (refusal of all worldly temptation). (2) The teacher's authority — Yama is the only possible teacher for this question, as Nachiketa proved. (3) The question's urgency — it is the universal human doubt (vicikitsā), asked on behalf of all beings (brūhi naḥ). (4) The impossibility of evasion — Yama has tried every deflection and failed. The stage is perfectly set. Valli 2 will begin with Yama's capitulation and the commencement of the greatest teaching in the Upanishads: the nature of the Self that is beyond death.
